en: The Compendium of Treatises, the First Chapter. 1.
An Exposition on Poetry (*Kāvyamīmāṃsā*), "The Illumination" (*Prakāśa*). Now begins the Secret of the Poet, the First Chapter.
1. The Compendium of Treatises.
Now, therefore, we shall investigate poetry (kāvya),
just as Śrīkaṇṭha taught it to the sixty-four [sages] beginning with Parameṣṭhin and Vaikuṇṭha;
and he, the Blessed One, [taught it] to his own disciples who were born by his mere will, who were self-existent (svayambhū).
Among them was Kāvyapuruṣa, the son of Agastya, who was worthy of worship even by the most eminent sages.

The Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), desiring the welfare of all beings dwelling in the three worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar, employed that knower of all systems— who could perceive future events with his divine eye— to initiate the science of poetry.
He taught the eighteen branches of learning in detail to the sons of the gods who were masters of the science of poetry;
among them, Sahasrākṣa compiled the *Kavirahasya*, and Uktigarbha the *Auktika*.
Suvarṇanābha [discussed] the determination of poetic styles (rīti), Pracetas [discussed] alliteration (ānuprāsika),
and Yama [discussed] the yamaka [rhyme].
Citrāṅgada [attained] Citra, Śeṣa [attained] śabdaśleṣa (the art of verbal punning), and Pulastya [attained] vāstuva (architecture).
Aupabhyama was the son of Upakāyana;
Parāśara excelled in *atiśaya*; and Ṛtadhya excelled in *arthaśleṣa*.
Kubera is the authority on both types of ornamentation; Kāmadeva is the authority on the erotic; and Bharata is the authority on the analysis of dramatic representation.
Nandikeśvara [taught] that which concerns aesthetic flavor (rasa),
Dhiṣaṇa that concerning defects (doṣa), and Upamanyu that concerning the employment of excellences (guṇa).
"The Upaniṣadic [teaching] is difficult to practice," they said;
thereupon, they each composed their own separate treatises.
And because it was thus scattered, that [Upaniṣadic teaching] became somewhat obscured.

Thus, this *Aṣṭādaśaprakaraṇī* has been composed, condensing the entire subject matter with few words while possessing the auxiliary members of the motivating purpose. This is the enumeration of its chapters and sections: 1. Summary of the Treatise (*śāstrasaṃgraha*).
2. The instruction on the treatise; 3. The origin of the Kāvyapuruṣa; 4. The intellectual brilliance of the disciples.
5. the results of linguistic analysis; 6. the discrimination of words and sentences;
7. the rules for sentence construction.
8. The types of interrogative intonation (kākuprakāra);
9. The establishment of recitation (pāṭhapratiṣṭhā); 10. The sources of the meaning of poetry (kāvyārthayoni).
11. Instruction on Meaning, 12. The Conduct of Poets, 13. The Conduct of Kings.
14. Methods of borrowing words and meanings; 15. Distinctions among poets; 16. Poetic conventions.
17. The division of place and time; 18. The structure of the universe; thus begins the first section, "The Secret of Poetry," and so forth.
Thus are the sūtras; now there will be a commentary (bhāṣya) explaining them.
This arrangement in both summary and detail is for our benefit as students.
This *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* of ours, rich with diverse illustrations yet concise in its composition, is the cause for the mastery of poetry.
This is that *Kāvyamīmāṃsā*, the investigation wherein even a fragment of speech is scrutinized;
he who does not know this does not truly understand even a fragment of speech.
Rājaśekhara, a follower of the Yāyāvara lineage, having condensed the extensive doctrines of the sages, has composed this *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* for the sake of poets.
Thus ends the first chapter, "The Compendium of the Treatise," in the first section, "The Secret of the Poet," of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.
___________________________ Chapter 2 _____________________________ Instruction on the Treatise (Śāstranirdeśa), the Second Chapter.
Regarding the instruction on the treatise: here, the literary word is twofold—namely, the scientific treatise (śāstra) and poetry (kāvyam).
Since poems are preceded by the sciences (*śāstra*), one should first apply oneself to the sciences.
That [science] is twofold: non-human (*apauruṣeya*) and human (*pauruṣeya*).
Non-human [science] is the Veda (*śruti*).
And that [Veda] consists of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa; those in which ritual actions are fully explained are the Mantras,
while the collection of texts concerning the praise, censure, explanation, application, and so forth of the Mantras is the Brāhmaṇa.
The three Vedas are the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma;
the Atharva is the fourth.
Among these, the Ṛcas are those verses whose metrical quarters (pādas) are established according to their meaning.
Those [verses] set to music are the Sāmans;
those without meters and not set to music are the Yajus;
and the Ṛks, Yajus, and Sāmans, together with the Atharvans—these are the four Vedas.

The Itihāsas, the Dhanurveda, and also the Gāndharvaveda and Āyurveda are the Upavedas. Drauṇi says: "The fifth is the Nāṭyaveda, which consists of the Vedas and Upavedas and pertains to all social classes. [Furthermore: "Śikṣā, Kalpa..."
grammar, etymology, and metrics;
"The Jyotiṣa and the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga)," say the teachers. "Because it is helpful, the Alaṅkāra is a true auxiliary science," says Yāyāvarīya;
for without a thorough understanding of its nature, there is no comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas.
As it is said:
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree;
one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating."
This is the statement of the treatise (*śāstra*).
In each section (*adhikaraṇa*), we shall cite examples from the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, *Sāmaveda*, *Atharvaveda*, and the *Brāhmaṇas*, and then provide examples in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*).

Among these, the *Śikṣā*—such as the *Āpiśalīya* and others—is that which determines the production of phonemes (*varṇa*) by means of their places of articulation (*sthāna*), points of formation (*karaṇa*), and degrees of effort (*prayatna*).
The *kalpa* is the aphoristic manual (*sūtra*) that prescribes the application of mantras studied in various Vedic branches;
it is the science of the *yajus*.
Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the systematic exposition of words.
Etymology (*nirvacana*) is *nirukta*; prosody (*chandas*), which provides instruction on Vedic meters, is *chandoviciti*; and astronomy (*jyotiṣa*) is the calculation of the planets (*grahagaṇita*).
The explanation of the ornaments (alaṅkāra) will follow later;
as for the Purāṇa, it is of human origin,
as is Ānvīkṣikī.
Mīmāṃsā and Smṛtitantra— these are the four branches of scripture. Among them, the Purāṇa, which consists primarily of narratives derived from the Vedas, is of eighteen kinds.
As they say: "That in which the creation, the dissolution, the eon, the intermediate periods of Manu, and the genealogies of the world are recorded— that is to be known as Purāṇa."
"Some maintain that 'itihāsa' is simply a specific division of the Purāṇas; and it is of two kinds, by way of accounts of others' deeds (parakriyā) and ancient cycles (purākalpa). As they say:"
"Parakriyā, Purākalpa, Itihāsa, and Gati are the fourfold divisions; the first has a single protagonist, while the second has many protagonists."
In this regard, the *Rāmāyaṇa* and the *Mahābhārata* serve as examples;
however, we shall discuss the science of *ānvīkṣikī* on the occasion of its specific treatment.
*Mīmāṃsā* is that which discriminates the sentences of the Vedas by means of thousands of logical arguments.
And that [scripture] is of two kinds: the analytical of injunctions (*vidhi-vivecana*) and the illustrative of Brahman (*brahma-nidarśinī*).
There are exactly eighteen traditional codes (*smṛtis*) because they are the recollections of the meaning of the Vedas (*śruti*). "These are the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*)."
"Namely, the four Vedas, the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), and the four treatises (śāstra)," so say the teachers.
These [sciences] exist by pervading even the entire triad of worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar.
Regarding this, they say:
"Even one who were to live for more than a thousand years would not be able to reach the end of the fields of knowledge."
Therefore, this collection of meanings has been stated in brief; the detailed expansion has been omitted for the sake of those who fear voluminous texts.
"Poetry (*kāvyam*) is the fifteenth field of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), being the sole abode of all fields of knowledge," says Yāyāvarīya;
for it consists of both prose and verse, it is the characteristic of poets, and it teaches what is beneficial and what is to be avoided. Furthermore, it follows after the [other] treatises.
"Vārttā, Kāmasūtra, Śilpaśāstra, and Daṇḍanīti—these, together with those mentioned previously, constitute the eighteen branches of knowledge," say some others.
"Ānvīkṣikī, Trayī, Vārttā, and Daṇḍanīti are the sciences," [say others].
"Daṇḍanīti alone is the single science," say the followers of Uśanas.
"Out of fear of punishment, the entire world remains established in its respective duties;
'Economics and the science of government are the two sciences,' say the followers of Bṛhaspati.
Livelihood and the acquisition of discipline are the causes for the stability of worldly life."
"The three sciences are the Trayī (the triple Vedas), Vārttā (economics), and Daṇḍanīti (polity)," so say the followers of Manu;
for the Trayī is the instructor of both Vārttā and Daṇḍanīti.
"The four sciences are Ānvīkṣikī (logic and metaphysics), Trayī, Vārttā, and Daṇḍanīti," says Kauṭilya.

"For it is through *ānvīkṣikī* (philosophical inquiry) that the *trayī* (the three Vedas) is discerned, and *vārttā* (economics) and *daṇḍanīti* (polity) attain their efficacy," says Yāyāvarīya. "The fifth is the science of literature (*sāhityavidyā*);
for it is the distillation of all four sciences."
That by which one may know both the Dharma and its purpose constitutes the science-nature (*vidyātva*) of the sciences.
Among these, the Trayī has been explained;
and the Anvīkṣikī is twofold, by way of the former and the latter sections.

In the view of the Arhat Bhadanta, the Lokāyata constitutes the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa), while Sāṃkhya and Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika constitute the final position (uttara-pakṣa). These are the six systems of reasoning (tarka).
In that regard, there are three types of discourse: debate (vāda), sophistry (jalpa), and cavil (vitaṇḍā).
Debate is the investigation of the reality of things for the sake of awakening to the truth between two neutral parties.

*Jalpa* (disputation) is the employment of quibbles, futile rejoinders, points of defeat, and so forth by one desiring victory in order to establish his own position. *Vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is that which does not establish its own position but merely seeks to refute the position of the opponent.
*Vārttā* (the means of livelihood) consists of agriculture, animal husbandry, and trade.
The *daṇḍa* (the power of punishment) is that which effects the acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) of *ānvīkṣikī*, *trayī*, and *vārttā*; its governance is *daṇḍanīti*.
The treatises [on this] maintain that the conduct of worldly life depends upon it.
And their general definition is as follows:
"Those undertakings of the scriptures which, like the currents of rivers, are insignificant at first but become increasingly vast as they progress, are worthy of reverence."
And their composition is by means of sūtras and so forth.
Among these, it is called a *sūtra* because of its concise formulation (*sūtraṇa*).
As they say:
"Those who know the composition of sūtras recognize them as being concise in syllables, free from ambiguity, substantial, comprehensive in all directions, devoid of filler, and irreproachable."
A *vṛtti* is a commentary that explains the entire essence of the *sūtras*.
A *paddhati* is an analysis of the *sūtras* and their *vṛttis*. A *bhāṣya* is so called because it speaks by way of raising objections (*ākṣipya*).
A *samīkṣā* is an internal commentary; it is that which provides an intermediate analysis of the meaning. A *ṭīkā* is a detailed explanation of the subject matter as far as possible.
The *pañjikā* is a commentary that analyzes difficult passages;
the *kārikā* is a verse that demonstrates the meaning;
and the *vārttika* is an investigation of what has been stated, what has not been stated, and what has been poorly stated—these are the divisions of treatises (*śāstra*).
"The poet of the treatise (śāstrakavi) proceeds by expanding upon a meaning that is obscure, clarifying what is submerged, transforming the small into the great, and the great into the small."

A *prakaraṇa* is the treatment of a single portion of a treatise (*śāstra*). As for chapters (*adhyāya*) and so forth, they are intermediate divisions composed by various authors independently; thus, they are innumerable and cannot be exhaustively named.
Knowledge consisting in the simultaneous presence of word and meaning exactly as they are is the *sāhityavidyā*.
The subsidiary sciences (*upavidyā*) are sixty-four; these are called the "arts" (*kalā*), according to the discourse of the learned. That constitutes the livelihood (*ājīva*) of poetry.
We shall discuss this in the *Tama-upaniṣad*.
Thus, an endless expansion of details regarding the learned in this matter has been omitted; it is accessible only to those of subtle intellect, for fear of making the book too voluminous.
Thus ends the second chapter, "Instruction on the Sciences," in the first section, "The Secret of the Poet," of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.
Chapter Three:
The Birth of the Kāvya-puruṣa.
Thus we have heard from our teachers these ancient and meritorious words concerning the birth of the Kāvya-puruṣa.

When the disciples, during the course of their discussion, asked that which remained as a lingering doubt— namely, "What kind of person is this Sarasvatī-son, the Poetic Spirit (Kāvyapuruṣa), who is your teacher?"—
he, the Lord of Great Speech (Bṛhatāmpati), spoke to them.
In ancient times, Sarasvatī, desiring a son, performed austerities on the Snowy Mountain.
Viriñca, with a pleased mind, said to her, "I shall create a son for you.
Thereupon, she gave birth to the Kāvya-puruṣa.
Rising up and grasping his feet, he uttered these words with devotion:
"O Mother, I am that very personification of poetry (Kāvyapumān) who manifests as this entire world consisting of speech; I bow at your feet."
Perceiving that seal of meter upon the subject of his speech— a thing previously seen only in the sacred scriptures— the Goddess joyfully took him onto her lap and said to him:
"My child, you who are the author of speech endowed with meter,
you seek out even me, your mother, as the mother of all verbal expression."
And they cite this as most praiseworthy: namely, "A defeat at the hands of one's son is a second birth of a son.
For the learned ones before you saw only prose, not verse;
from this point on, however, speech endowed with meter shall proceed, originating from you.
Oh, you are truly praiseworthy! Words and their meanings are your body, and refined Sanskrit is your mouth.
The *prakṛta* [mudrā] is the arms; the *aparabhraṃśa* is the hips;
the *paiśāca* is the feet; and the *miśra* is the chest.
You are even, serene, sweet, noble, and full of vigor;
your speech is eloquent, and its essence is flavor.
The meters are beautiful, and verbal play consisting of riddles, questions and answers, and so forth, as well as alliteration, similes, and other figures of speech, adorn you.
Even the Śruti, expressing a future matter, praises you:
"He has four horns, three feet, and seven hands on his head;
bound in three ways, the bull bellows loudly; the great god has entered into mortals."

"Nevertheless, conceal the deed of this audacious man and act in a manner befitting a child," she said, and having placed him upon a bed of rock-slab surfaces beneath a tree, she went to bathe in the celestial Gaṅgā.
Meanwhile, the great sage Uśanas, who had gone out to gather *kuśa* grass and sacrificial fuel, saw him drenched by the heat as the sun turned back.
Thinking, "Whose helpless child is this? he led him to his own hermitage.
Having recovered his breath in an instant, that son of Sarasvatī imparted to him speech endowed with the Vedas.
Startling him suddenly, he spoke:
"May that Sarasvatī, the cow of speech, who— though milked daily by various milkers— is as if never milked, dwell within our hearts."
Thus he spoke;
and he ordained for his students that they should attain the higher worlds preceded by that [knowledge].
From that time forth, the virtuous call that Uśanas "Kavi."
And because of that metaphorical application, the worldly convention is "the poets are poets.
Furthermore, the word *kavi* is derived from the root *kavṛ*, meaning "to describe," which has poetry (*kāvyakarma*) as its object.
And because Sarasvatī’s son is essentially identical to poetry, people figuratively apply the term "Poetic Man" (*kāvyapuruṣa*) to him.

Then the Goddess of Speech, having turned back and not seeing her son there, wailed from the depths of her heart. And Vālmīki, the bull among sages, who had arrived there by chance, respectfully related that news to the Blessed Lady and showed her the hermitage of Bhṛgu’s son.
She too, her breasts flowing with milk, embracing her son and kissing his head, with a tranquil mind, bestowed words accompanied by the Vedic meters even upon the great seer Vālmīki;
and having been sent away by her, he, filled with grief upon beholding a young female Krauñca bird crying out with a piteous cry for her mate slain by a Niṣāda, uttered this verse:
"O Niṣāda, may you find no rest for eternal years!"
Because you slew one of a pair of cranes while it was deluded by passion.

Then the goddess, possessing divine vision, granted a boon even for that verse, namely: "Whoever, having studied no other [work], shall study this first, he shall become a poet possessed of the grace of Sarasvatī.
That great sage, his speech having begun, composed the epic history known as the Rāmāyaṇa.
Dvaipāyana, however, was a student of the first verse; by its power, he [composed] the *Bhārata*, a compendium of one hundred thousand verses.
Once, during a dispute over the Vedas between a host of Brahman-sages and the gods, the self-existent God, out of courtesy, appointed him as the arbiter of this matter.
Having heard the account, he followed his mother as she was walking away.

"Child, since you have not been authorized by Parameṣṭhin, your journey to the world of Brahmā will not lead to the highest good," saying this, she forcibly turned him back; yet he proceeded by his own will.
Thereupon, that Kāvyapuruṣa departed in anger.
And his dear friend Kumāra was addressed with a cry by Gaurī as she wept: "O Father!"
"Be silent; I shall restrain her," she declared, and reflected:
"For living beings, there is generally no bond other than love.

Therefore, in order to bring this man under control, I shall create a certain woman. Thinking thus, she brought forth the bride of the science of poetry (Sāhityavidyā) and commanded her: "This husband of Dharma stands before you in anger."
Therefore, follow him and turn him back; come now,
O venerable sages!

"O you who have completed your studies in the science of poetry, praise this life-story of these two; for this shall become the very essence of your poetic art," said the blessed goddess Bhavānī, and then she became silent.
They too resolved to do so.
Then they all first proceeded toward the eastern direction, where the regions of Aṅga, Vaṅga, Suhma, Brahmapuṇḍra, and others are located.
There, applying herself to that which is beyond measure, she assumed whatever dress she desired,
and she was followed by the women of that place;
her conduct was that of a Raudra-Māgadhī.
The sages praised her:

"May this attire— featuring a pearl necklace resting upon moist sandalwood-paste-smeared breasts, a garment kissing the parting of the hair, and clearly revealing the base of the arms— shine for a long time among the women of Gauḍa, who possess the luster of fresh *dūrvā* grass due to their constant enjoyment of aloe wood."
Whatever kind of costume that son of Sarasvatī happened to wear, the men there assumed that same attire;
her manner of movement was also exactly like his.
Furthermore, whatever dancing, instrumental music, and so forth she performed constituted the Bhāratī style (vṛtti).

"O sages, that [speech] of yours... and so on, as is the same as the preceding [definition]. That mode of composition (*rīti*) is the Gauḍīyā, which consists of a sentence containing compounds, alliteration (*anuprāsa*), and the internal inclusion of *yoga-vṛtti* (etymological derivation), even though it has been rendered powerless by such a construction.
"That [gift] of yours, O sages," and so on, is the same as the preceding [passage].
We shall explain the nature of the mode of conduct and style (vṛttirīti) at the appropriate occasion. And then he set out toward the Pañcālas.
Where there are the territories of the Pañcālas, Śūrasenas, Hastināpura, Kaśmīra, Vāhīka, Bāhlīka, Bāhlaveya, and so forth;
there, when one applies [the rules], it is "tamaumeyī," which is the same as the previous case.
That is the application in the middle of the Pañcāla region.
The sages praised her thus:

"Bow down to the attire of these women of great splendor— whose cheeks are rippled by the swaying of their earrings, who wear shimmering pearl necklaces hanging to the navel, and whose lower garments circle from the hips down to the ankles."
When he whose attire was somewhat moistened by emotion was that son of Sarasvatī, it is the same as before;

she too was that very same [goddess], which is the same as before. When she displayed a slight degree of dance, song, instrumental music, graceful gestures, and so forth, that is the Sāttvatī style (vṛtti).
Because it possesses a winding movement, it is *ārabhaṭī*;
"that [speech] of yours, O sages," and so on, is identical with the previous [verse].

Even though that [speech] was composed in such a manner, if a sentence were made slightly discordant—being somewhat unbalanced, somewhat lacking in alliteration, and filled with figurative expressions—then...
She spoke in the Pāñcālī style; "those sages said to her" and so forth is the same as before. Thereupon, he set out toward the Avantis.
Where there are the territories of Avanti, Vaidiśa, Surāṣṭra, Mālava, Arbuda, Bhṛgu, Kaccha, and so forth— there,
attacking him, [one should say] "This is an Aumeyī," as before.
That *vṛtti* is Āvantī;
for it moves between the Pāñcāla-madhyama and the Dākṣiṇātya styles.
For this very reason, the Sātvatī and Kaiśikī *vṛttis* are present therein.
The sages praised her, saying:
"May the fashioning of dress for men flourish among the Pāñcālas, while that of women may rejoice in the South;
but in the land of Avanti, whatever is spoken and whatever conduct is observed is a blending of both."
Then he reached the southern direction,
where there are the Masaya, Ekalavya, Mañjara, and other mountain ranges, as well as the territories of Kuntala, Kerala, Mahārāṣṭra, Gāṅga, Kaliṅga, and others.
Regarding that, they apply [the term] "tamaumeyī," which is the same as the previous [case];
that is the southern usage.
The sages praised her:

"Victorious for a long time is this poison of the Kerala women, whose beautiful crest has locks of hair curling from the roots, whose forehead is marked by a mass of powdered curls, and whose waist-knot is tightened by being tucked into the side of the garment."
With his mind enamored of her, he appeared in such attire that he was like the son of Sarasvatī; this is the same as what was stated previously.
She too was the very same [as described] before; this is the same as what was stated previously.
That which she manifested—consisting of various dances, songs, instrumental music, graceful gestures, and so forth—is the Kaiśikī Vṛtti.
"O sages, that [speech] of yours..."—the rest is the same as before.

And because he was exceedingly brought under her control, he spoke words characterized by *sthāna* (place), *anuprāsa* (alliteration), absence of compounds (*asamāsa*), and containing *yogavṛtti* (elliptical or metaphorical application);
that is the Vaidarbha style (*rīti*).
"O sages, that [is] yours"— the rest is the same as before.
In this context, *pravṛtti* is the sequence of arranging attire,
while *vṛtti* is the sequence of arranging graceful gestures.

*Rīti* (style) is the arrangement of the sequence of words. Regarding this, the Teachers [the *Ācāryas*] have said: "The modes of speech and the manners of action are fourfold, whereas countries are infinite; how, then, can they be grasped in their entirety? For even though countries are infinite, they conceive of them as being only fourfold. Yāyāvarīya, however, maintains: "In general, there is the domain of a universal monarch (*cakravartikṣetra*), but by its internal subdivisions, they are indeed infinite."
From the southern ocean toward the northern direction, for a thousand *yojanas*, is the realm of the universal monarch (*cakravartin*);
therein alone is the rule for attire.
Beyond that, even those who are divine and so forth should be depicted assuming the dress characteristic of whichever region they inhabit.
But within one's own realm, there is freedom of action;
for those born in other continents, their livelihoods and activities proceed according to that [custom]. Furthermore, there are three types of conduct, which are described below.
There, in the land of Vidarbha, is a city named Vatsagulma, the pleasure-resort of the god Manojanman (Kāmadeva).
There, the son of Sarasvatī (Bṛhaspati) married that daughter of Umā (Umā’s daughter) according to the Gandharva rite.
Then, having returned from that wedding and wandering through those regions, he arrived at the very Snowy Mountain (Himavat).
There, Gaurī and Sarasvatī stood as mutual companions;

having been saluted by the couple, they bestowed their blessings and, with bodies composed of splendor, made them dwellers in the minds of poets. And they fashioned that creation of theirs into a heavenly realm for poets.
Wherein poets, dwelling among mortals with a body composed of poetry, rejoice for an eon with a divine form—
thus was this Kāvya-puruṣa created of old by the Self-existent One;
knowing him thus through such a division, one rejoices both hereafter and in this world.
Thus ends the third chapter, "The Origin of the Kāvya-puruṣa," in the first section, "The Secret of the Poet," of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.
Chapter Four:
The Pupil’s Genius The Fourth Chapter: The Pupil’s Genius.
They describe two kinds of disciples: namely, the intelligent (*buddhimān*) and the one of acquired intelligence (*āhāryabuddhi*).
He whose intellect naturally pursues the treatise is the intelligent one;
and he whose intellect is refined through the practice of the treatise is the one of acquired intelligence.
And that [wisdom] is threefold: mindfulness, intelligence, and discernment.
Mindfulness is that which remembers an object already passed.
The intellect (*mati*) is the counselor for the present;
wisdom (*prajñā*) is the foreknower of the future. Though it is of these three kinds, it is beneficial to poets.
Of these two, the one with intelligence serves [the teacher], listens, grasps, retains, understands, deliberates, refutes [objections], and penetrates the reality.
These same qualities belong to the one of "trainable" intellect as well, but they depend upon an instructor.
Daily attendance upon a true guru is the preeminent quality for both of them.
For that [learning] is indeed the wish-fulfilling cow for the expansion of the intellect.
Regarding this, they say:
"In the grasping of objects as they truly are, it first spreads the light of wisdom; thereafter, it produces a mind made lucid by the activity of reasoning and refutation."
Therefore, one should not settle into [worldly] attachments; that reality arises through a single gateway, and through gradual acquaintance with those advanced in knowledge, it leads to immortality.
One who possesses a contrary understanding toward these two is of poor intellect.
Among them, the practice belongs to the intelligent one.
Indeed, he who has understood the meaning upon a single exposition should attend the preceptor’s household to seek the path of the poets.
For one of pliable intellect, however, there are two states: non-comprehension and doubt.
Such a person would attend upon teachers in order to comprehend the matter not yet understood and to dispel doubt.
For one of corrupt intellect, on the other hand, there is simply a perversion of the mind regarding everything.

For that [inspiration], being like a garment variegated with indigo, cannot have any further qualities added to it; therefore, if the power of Sarasvatī favors it, we shall discuss that under the section on the Upaniṣads.
Śyāmadeva maintains that "the poet’s concentration (samādhi) is what exerts the greatest effort in the work of poetry.
Concentration is the one-pointedness of the mind.
A concentrated mind perceives the true nature of objects; as it has been said:
"The power of Sarasvatī is an indescribable, supreme secret, beyond the reach of the senses, and to be cultivated exclusively by the skillful among the wise.
For its attainment, this is the supreme means: the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of a mind that has mastered all that is to be known."
"Practice" (*abhyāsa*) is auspicious;
practice is the continuous cultivation [of a skill].
For it leads everywhere and bestows unsurpassed proficiency in all things.
Internal effort is concentration (*samādhi*), while external effort is practice (*abhyāsa*);
both of these bring forth power.
"That alone is the cause," says Yāyāvarīya.
And that diffusion [of knowledge] occurs through intuition (*pratibhā*) and proficiency (*vyutpatti*).
For intuition and proficiency are the two objects of action for the agent that is capacity (*śakti*);
that which possesses capacity has intuition, and that which possesses capacity becomes proficient.

That which causes the entire range of words, the multitude of meanings, the system of ornaments, the path of liberation, and whatever else of that kind appears within the heart is *pratibhā* (intuition).
To one who lacks *pratibhā*, the multitude of objects is as if beyond perception; but for one possessed of *pratibhā*, it is as if directly perceived, even though they do not actually see it.
For it is heard that Megha, Āvirudrakumāra, Dāsa, and others were poets born blind;
furthermore, even great poets have composed descriptions of the customs of other countries and islands based on their observations of people from those places.
Among these, the customs of other countries are as follows:

In a forest where the wish-fulfilling trees abound, they maintain their livelihood by means of the vital breath; they perform the rite of holy ablution in waters tawny with the pollen of golden lotuses;
they practice meditation in jeweled stone chambers and self-restraint in the presence of celestial women—that which other sages desire through their austerities, these [ascetics] practice right here.
The commerce of other islands: Dwell with him on the shores of the ocean, rustling with groves of palm trees,
where the breezes— having dispelled every trace of perspiration with cloves brought from other islands— caress you.
The discourse on the conduct of men: Even Hara, his composure shaken like the ocean at the onset of moonrise,
cast his eyes upon Umā’s face, with its lower lip like the fruit of the *bimba*.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera"—a female companion, preceded by a jest, spoke to her friend who was like a Tathāgata:
"O girl, let us go elsewhere. Then the bridegroom’s wife looked at her with a frown of resentment.
And that [inspiration] is twofold: the producer and the cultivator.
The producer is that which assists the poet;
it is also threefold: innate, acquired, and instructional.
The innate [wisdom] depends on the latencies from previous lives;
the acquired arises from the latencies of this life;
and the instructional originates from the instructions of mantra, tantra, and so forth.

They designate that first [type of faith] as "innate" (*sahaja*) when it is produced by even a slight degree of worldly refinement; however, when produced by a great degree [of refinement], it is "acquired" (*āhāryā*). Furthermore, for the "instructional" (*aupadeśikī*) type, the time of instruction occurs precisely in this life.
The time for refinement occurs in this very life.
These three types of poets are: the Sārasvata, the Ābhyāsika, and the Pāra-yātrika.
And there is that which is derived from instruction.
One who possesses eloquence set in motion by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previous births is "Sārasvata" (gifted with Sarasvatī), being endowed with intelligence.
One whose speech is illuminated by practice in this very life is "Ābhyāsika" (gifted through practice), possessing acquired intelligence (*āhāryabuddhi*).
"One of poor intellect who possesses the power of speech only through what has been taught and shown is called *aupadeśika* (one who relies on instruction).
Therefore, the other two [types of practitioners] do not require the remaining parts of the *tantra*.
For the teachers say: 'The grape, naturally sweet, does not depend upon the refinement of molasses.'"
"No," says Yāyāvarīya;
for two actions directed toward a single purpose result in a doubling [of effort].
"Among them, each preceding one is superior," says Śyāmadeva.
The *sārasvata* [speech] is independent and free from defects; the *ābhyāsika* is measured;
while the *aupadeśaka* here may be charming, trivial, or even mere chatter.
"Superiority is better," says Yāyāvarīya; and that occurs when there is a conjunction of many qualities. Furthermore—
"Intelligence, the practice of training in the arts that are limbs of poetry,
and the poet's secret power— this triad is difficult to find together in one place."
For the wise one who has practiced poetry and the sciences that are its limbs,
and who is devoted to the performance of mantras, the status of a king among poets is most near.
This is a common saying regarding the relative gradations among poets:
"The poetry of one poet remains in his very home; that of another travels as far as the houses of his friends."
Placing his feet constantly upon the faces of those who are unrefined, he wanders about like one curious to see everything.

This [poetic expression] is the creator; it is the bringer-into-being (bhāvayitrī) because it assists the one who brings [the work] into being. For it brings to life both the labor and the intention of the poet.
Indeed, by her [the Muse], the poet’s tree of activity has borne fruit;
otherwise, it would be barren. "What, then, is the difference between these two, such that the poet creates and the connoisseur (*bhāvaka*) is also a poet? ask the teachers. Regarding this, they say:
"According to the gradations of their creative intuition (*pratibhā*), the establishment [of poetry] on earth is manifold;
however, the poet who is a true *bhāvaka* generally does not fall into an inferior state."

"No," said Kālidāsa; "for the state of being a *bhāvaka* (an evocative artist) is indeed distinct from the state of being a poet (*kavitva*), and the state of being a poet is distinct from the state of being a *bhāvaka*."
This is due to the difference in their essential natures and the difference in their objects.
As they say:
"One is able to compose speech, while another is only able to hear it; your auspicious intellect excites our wonder in both respects."
For excellences do not converge in a single place; one [element] produces gold, while another is capable of testing it.
"Furthermore, they are of two kinds: those who do not disclose [their faults] and those who consume even grass," says Maṅgala.
"There are also poets," say the followers of Vāmana.
"Of four kinds," says Yāyāvarīya: "the envious and those intent on [knowing] reality.
Regarding this, Vāmanīya says: "The former are the discerning; those immediately following them are the opposite of that.
For their lack of interest is innate.
Or rather, it has its source in knowledge.
For they do not abandon their innate dross, even by means of a hundred refinements, just as tin does not lose its blackness;
however, regarding that speech which possesses a source in knowledge and is endowed with distinguished wisdom, there is simply a natural inclination toward it—so says Yāyāvarīya.
Furthermore, the consumption of even grass is common to all;
for instance, for everyone who is desirous of knowledge and full of curiosity, this [consumption] occurs first everywhere.
Indeed, a lack of discernment in one's intuition does not allow the thread of distinction between merit and demerit to be cast down.
Then one abandons much and grasps much;
for when the intellects flow like honey in accordance with seclusion (*viveka*),
one becomes a seer of reality (*yathārthadarśin*) upon its transformation.
The removal of delusion establishes supreme bliss;
however, for the envious, even that which has become manifest does not manifest, because they maintain silence regarding the virtues of others.
Furthermore, such a person is free from envy and is rarely found.
As it has been said:
"Who are you, sir? I am a poet. What fresh verse might be recited, my friend? Let the talk of poetry be abandoned for now; why should this be heard by me?"
He who correctly discerns the essence of faults and virtues is himself a true poet; such a person exists as a connoisseur in this world, or perhaps by chance there may be one who is free from envy.
But as for one who is intent upon the true nature [of poetry], if there be but one among a thousand, it has been said:

"He who discerns the arrangements of words, rejoices in the compositions of eloquent sayings, sips the thick nectar of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and investigates both the literal meaning and the underlying intention (*tātparya*);

such a person, a knower of the toil of poetry, encounters [this state] only through merits, at some time and only for certain wise men who, due to the absence of other discerners, are inwardly distressed."
One's own son, a friend, a minister, a disciple, and even a teacher—these five are the treasury of a poet; for what is there that he cannot bring to life?
Of what use is the poetry of that poet whose compositions are not carried to the ten directions by connoisseurs, remaining instead as mere fluctuations within his own mind?
In every house there are compositions of poetry deposited in books; but only two or three have been engraved upon the stone slabs of the hearts of connoisseurs.
In a true poem, certain transformations of the spectator’s soul arise,
which were not even perceived by the Creator of Drama when determining all the modes of representation.
One may be an evoker through speech, another an evoker through the heart,
and yet another an evoker through sattvic physical gestures and consequent expressions.
One practitioner is intent on taking up virtues; another is intent on taking up faults;
and yet another practitioner is intent on both taking up and abandoning virtues and faults.
Since this sequence is so diverse despite the charge being the same,
we know that the cause for men's favor here is superhuman.
He who is neither a natural poet nor one refined in the sciences, yet composes poetry,
truly mocks himself by being possessed by an obsessive obsession.
For one in whom poetic talent does not reside and who has merely performed artificial displays of skill in poetry,
success through Sarasvatī comes from the application of tantras and mantras.
When the wise man perceives the distinction between his own words and the words of others,
then he should be considered either a perfected master or a mere bad poet.
"Kārayitrī (the Causer) and Bhāvayitrī (the Inspirer)—these are the two divisions of Pratibhā (Inspiration).
Now, therefore, we shall explain Vyutpatti (Mastery), the mother of poetry."
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Explanation of the Student’s Creative Genius," in the first section, "The Secret of the Poet," of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.
Chapter Five:
The Maturation of the Poet through Cultivation (*Vyutpatti*)
The Fifth Chapter: 5.
The Maturation of Cultivation. "Cultivation is extensive knowledge," say the teachers;
for the words of poets extend in every direction.
As it has been said:
"Whose speech does not expand in some way toward even the most familiar subject? That alone is true poetic power whereby one's words reach in every direction."
“Discrimination between what is appropriate and inappropriate is proficiency,” says Yāyāvarīya. “Between intuition and proficiency, intuition is superior,” says Ānanda;
for intuition completely covers over every defect caused by a poet’s lack of proficiency.
Regarding this, it is said:
"The defect caused by a lack of proficiency is concealed by the poet's power;
however, that which is caused by a lack of ability appears immediately as a flaw."
And this word "capacity" (*śakti*) is used figuratively for "intuition" (*pratibhā*). As for intuition—for example:
"What is this that is situated on the head of my father?"
"Is this a fragment of the moon? Is this the forehead? Is this an eye?

Are these serpents in his hand?"—may the smile of the Goddess, beautiful as she rests her left hand upon the shoulder of the trident-bearing Śiva as he poses these questions in succession to the naked Krauñca-foe, protect you.
“Mastery [of language] is superior,” so says Maṅgala;
for that indeed covers every defect caused by the poet’s lack of skill.
As it is said:
"The lack of proficiency of a poet on the path of poetry is concealed by his erudition; however, for those whose minds are set on discernment, the mere stringing together of words is to be rejected."
An example of *vyutpatti* (erudition):
"A golden necklace was placed upon her neck, yet no slender string of gems; a delicate lotus-leaf was set behind her ear, yet no ornamented earring;
she wore no variegated silk garment, but rather a pure white one—by the young woman, as the pleasures of love drew near."
“Imagination and erudition, when combined, are mutually beneficial,” says Yāyāvarīya.
Indeed, the attainment of charm without a perfection of form, or a perfection of form without the attainment of charm, does not lead to great beauty. Their union is as follows:

Victorious is the fresh staff-like foot of Bhavānī, which, with its shanks like lotus stalks and toes radiant with the filaments of her toenail-rays, possesses sprouts in the form of the spreading luster of fresh lac-dye and bees in the form of her charming anklets; it creates the beauty of a lotus born from the pond of the natural, transparent loveliness of her own body during the imitation of her husband’s dance.
A poet who possesses both creative intuition (*pratibhā*) and proficiency (*vyutpatti*) is called a "poet" (*kavi*).
He is of three kinds:
the scholar-poet (*śāstrakavi*), the poet-poet (*kāvyakavi*), and the poet of both (*ubhayakavi*).
"Among them, each subsequent one is more important," says Śyāmadeva. "No," says Yāyāvarīya;
"each is more important within its own respective domain."
For the royal swan is not capable of drinking moonlight, nor is the cakora bird able to extract milk from water; likewise,
a scholar-poet who interrupts the perfection of rasa in a poem [is ineffective].
The poet of poetry softens even a meaning that is harsh with logic in a technical treatise through the variety of his expression;
however, the poet of both is superior to both, provided he is highly proficient in both fields. Therefore, the poets of the treatise and of poetry are indeed equal in power.
We do, however, acknowledge a mutual relationship of benefit and beneficiary between the treatise (śāstra) and poetry (kāvyam).
For while the refinement of the treatise favors poetry, exclusive devotion to the treatise restrains it;
likewise, the refinement of poetry conforms to the ripening of the sentences of the treatise, whereas exclusive devotion to poetry obstructs it.
In this regard, the poet of the treatise (śāstrakavi) is of three kinds:
he who composes a treatise, and he who composes poetry within a treatise.
Furthermore, even he who incorporates the meaning of a treatise into poetry is a poet of poetry;
moreover, such a poet is of eight kinds, namely: the poet of composition (*racanākavi*),...
A poet of words, a poet of meaning,
and a poet of ornamentation.
the poet of speech,
the poet of rasa, and the poet of style;
Regarding the phrase "the poet of the meaning of the treatise" (*śāstrārthakavi*): therein, the poet of composition (*racanākavi*) is as follows:
"With the cries of the langurs, who form circles upon the trunks of the bakula trees entwined by their swaying vine-like tails, the ancient cave-dwellings resound with echoes."

In the groves, the fragrant winds blew along the shore, carrying the scent of uddaṇṭa, piṇḍī, and tagara flowers; having overstepped the boundary, they caused the stalks of the lotus ponds to burst open with force.
And the poet of words (śabdakavi) is threefold, according to the distinction of nouns (nāman), verbs (ākhyāta), and both.
Among these, the poet of nouns (nāmakavi) is as follows:
"Like learning for a man, like majesty for a king, like wisdom for a physician, like compassion for a virtuous man..."
She alone was the modesty of that hero, the grace of the youth, and the very ornament of that king.
An example by the poet Ākhyātaka:
"They laughed most loudly, rejoiced, roared, and struck [one another] with their quivering masses of arms;
they offered praises, were filled with joy, and held in high esteem the words of their guru, which contained within them the attainment of the source of nectar."
The poet Nāmākhyātaka says:

"With their luster destroyed, blind, their shoulders and arms limp, as if deprived of consciousness by despair, the women for a moment did not cry out, nor weep, nor utter a sound, nor move; they were like figures drawn in a painting."
The poet Arthakaṣi says:

"May the sound protect you—the sound produced by the clashing of their thick, aged bones as they strike one another’s laps, a sound that surpasses the deep resonance of the gods’ drums, arising when Cāmuṇḍā, her arms raised high, embraces Bhṛṅgiriṭi at the joyful cry of 'The Goddess has given birth to a son! Dance, O Gaṇas! Why do you stand still?'"
The poet of ornamentation is twofold, distinguished by word and meaning. Of these two, the verbal ornament is as follows:
"I did not meet with an untimely death; rather, through my sinful deed, I met with an untimely death."
"I did not die in the Bhāgīrathī; having embraced a street, I, unfortunate as I am, have died."
Arthālaṅkāra (Poetic Figure of Sense): "My arm is capable of depriving Vāsuki— whose parasol is his hood and whose banner is his flickering tongue— of the poverty of his tooth-picks."
The poet Uktikavi says:
"This belly is blameless, to be licked by the sighs of proud women; the expanse of her breast-slopes is the limit for the licking of creeper-like arms;
and the moon of her face shines forth, to be drunk from by the channels of her glances. Thus, in this fair-eyed woman, the playful sports of youth flourish."
Or as it is said:
"The lower lip receives the transformation of the *āśoka* bud; the cheek descends into the state of a pale *tāḍī* leaf;
the gaze imitates the lotus that is almost withered; thus she touches upon sweetness and attains thinness."
Rasaka-vi says:
"O slender-waisted one, behold this Tāmraparṇī river as it flows into the ocean;
from its waters, pearls are extracted by the opened shells of oysters, which then transform into necklaces upon the swelling breasts of beautiful women."
Mārgakavi says:

"The roots of young creepers, the fragrant bark of *jātī* trees, the heartwood of sandalwood and *sāśina* trees, the fresh sprouts of the *aśoka*, the first blossoms of the *śirīṣa*, and the ripening *moca* fruit— this very collection, which removes the heat, was formerly given by Summer to the five-arrowed god [Kāma] when he had been consumed by fire."
The poet Śāstrārthaka says:

"Those who delight in the Self, whose pleasure is fixed in unwavering meditative absorption (samādhi), whose knots of darkness are severed by the overflow of knowledge, and who are established in pure being—they behold that indescribable One who stands beyond both darkness and light. How can this man, blinded by delusion, know that ancient God?"
Among these, one possessing two or three qualities is a minor poet, one with five is mediocre, and one endowed with all the qualities is a great poet.
And there are ten stages of the poet; among them,
six belong to those of innate intelligence and acquired intelligence,
and three to the instructional poet.
Namely: one who has mastered the science of poetry,
a poet of the heart,
and one who speaks of others.
One who has practiced, one who is striving, and a great poet.
The king of poets,
the one who causes no interruption,
and the transmitter.

He who, desiring poetic skill, attends the teachers' households to acquire the primary and secondary sciences of poetry is a *vidyāsnātaka*. He who composes poetry only within his own heart and conceals it is a *hṛdayakavi*.
He who recites even his own poem by attributing it to another out of fear of faults is an *anyāpadeśin*.
He who practices the style of any one of the easterners and whose speech is fluent is a *sevita* (practitioner).
He who composes faultless verses but does not compose extended compositions is a *ghaṭamāna* (striver). He who is proficient in composing either [type] is a *mahākavi* (great poet).
But he who is independent in various specific linguistic registers, in those various compositions, and in each particular aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), is a king among poets;
such individuals, even in this world, are but few.
He who composes poetry at the very moment of being possessed by a deity through the power of instructions regarding mantras and so forth is one who composes through possession (*āveśika*).
One who speaks without interruption whenever he desires is an "uninterrupted" speaker (*avicchedin*).
One who, having mastered mantras over girls, boys, and so forth, causes Sarasvatī to transfer into them is a "transmitter" (*saṅkrāmayitṛ*).
Through the power of constant practice, the speech of a skilled poet attains maturity (*pāka*).
"But what is this ripening? ask the teachers; "It is transformation," says Maṅgala.
"What, then, is this *pariṇāma*?
ask the Teachers (*ācāryas*). "The hearing of nouns and verbs; such is this derivation (*vyutpatti*)," says Maṅgala.
This is excellence of diction (*sauśabdya*). "The firmness of word-placement is *pāka*," say the Teachers.
Thus they have said:
As long as the mind wavers between inserting and removing words, alas, Sarasvatī remains unaccomplished; but once the stability of the words has been established, she is truly mastered.

"Because it results in the stability of the words even through the grasping and holding [of their meanings], the maturity (*pāka*) of words is their aversion to substitution (*parivṛtti*)," so say the followers of Vāmana.
As they have said:
"Those words which truly abandon the capacity for substitution..."
Those proficient in the application of words call that the ripening of word-usage.
"This is a lack of power, not yet ripeness," says Avantisundarī.
Since even among great poets there is no single reading that attains full ripeness regarding a single subject,
therefore *pāka* (ripeness) consists in the composition of words and meanings suited to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
As he said: "That sequence of the arrangement of qualities, ornaments, styles, expressions, words, and meanings,
by which it is relished by the wise— that, for me, is the ripeness of a sentence."
As it has been said:
"When there is a speaker, when there is a true subject matter, when there is the word, and when there is aesthetic flavor (rasa)—
there exists that [poetry] without which the honey of speech does not flow forth."

"Since it is to be inferred from its effects, that supreme *pāka* (culmination) which is conveyed by the words 'it' (*tat*) and 'that' (*tad*) is indeed the domain of denotation; established solely through the consensus of connoisseurs (*sahr̥daya*), it serves as a constituent of literary usage"—so says Yāyāvarīya.
And that [culmination], when a poet practices his craft, becomes ninefold.
Among these, that which is tasteless at the beginning and end is called *picumandapāka*.

The ripening of the jujube fruit is insipid at first and middling in its final stage; the ripening of the grape is insipid at first but sweet in its final stage; and the ripening of the eggplant is middling at first but insipid in the end.
The tamarind fruit has a middling taste at the beginning and end; the mango fruit is middling at the beginning and sweet at the end;
and the areca nut fruit is excellent at the beginning and insipid at the end.

That which is excellent at the beginning and middling at the end is called "tin-ripening" (trapusapāka); that which is sweet at both the beginning and the end is called "coconut-ripening" (nālikerapāka).
Among these three groups of three, the ripenings in the first [group] are to be abandoned.
It is better not to be a poet at all than to be a bad poet; for bad poetry is death with gasping breath. Those who are mediocre should be refined.
For refinement enhances the quality of everything;
even gold of twelve colors becomes pure gold through heating in fire. The rest should be understood accordingly.
For that which is pure by nature does not depend upon refinement;
a whetstone cannot produce greater brilliance in a pearl.
On the other hand, they describe the ripening of the wood-apple as being unstable.
In this regard, just as one obtains grains of rice by winnowing straw, so too does one obtain well-spoken verses;
for one who practices correctly, poetry ripens in nine ways.
Therefore, a wise person should analyze it according to the Sūtra on Rejection and Acceptance.
This threefold procedure has been shown here specifically for disciples;
however, this very diversity also exists throughout the triple world.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the description of the learned poet and the poet by temperament, in the first section, the Secret of the Poet, within the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.
Chapter Six:
The Analysis of Words and Sentences (Padavākyaviveka) 6

The analysis of words and sentences: A word is that which is determined by the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*), and its denoted meaning is that which is indicated by etymology (*nirukta*), glossaries (*nighaṇṭu*), and so forth; these two constitute a *pada*. It has five modes of formation (*vṛtti*): the mode of nominal inflection (*subvṛtti*) and the mode of compound formation (*samāsavṛtti*).
The derivative formation (taddhita-vṛtti), the verbal derivative formation (kṛd-vṛtti), and the finite verb formation (tiṅ-vṛtti).
Words denoting genus include "fair-skinned," "horse," "man," and "elephant.
Words denoting substance include "Hara," "Hari," "Hiraṇyagarbha," "time," "space," and "direction.
And words denoting quality include "white," "black," "red," and "yellow."
Terms such as *pācaka* (cook) and *pāṭhaka* (reader) denote action; *prādayaḥ* (the group beginning with pra) and *cādayaḥ* (the group beginning with ca) denote non-substances (*asattvavacana*).
Terms such as *nagaram upa prasthitaḥ panthāḥ* (the path leading toward the city) and *vṛkṣam anu dyotate vidyut* (the lightning flashes along the tree) are termed *karmapravacanīya*.
"The fivefold *sub-vṛtti* is indeed the mother of all verbal expression (*vāṅmaya*)," so say the learned.
*Sub-vṛtti* itself is *samāsa-vṛtti*;
expansion (*vyāsa*) and contraction (*samāsa*) are the causes of their distinction.
And that [compound] is sixfold, distinguished by the *dvandva* and other types.
Regarding this, the *Ṣaṭpadasamāsīsamāsa-sūkta* states: "I am the *dvandva*, I am the *dvigu*, and in my house there is always the *avyayībhāva*."
Therefore, O friend, maintain that *tatpuruṣa* compound by which I may become a *bahuvrīhi*.
Furthermore, the application of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) is infinite;
for it is a common saying in the treatises that "the followers of Pāṇini are confounded by secondary suffixes.
Examples ending in secondary suffixes include *māñjiṣṭha*, *raucanika*, *saura*, *saindhava*, and *vaiyāsīya*.
This [function] has the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as its domain,
whereas the operation of *kṛt* suffixes has the verbal root (*dhātu*) as its domain;
for example, "agent" (*kartṛ*), "remover" (*hartṛ*), "potter" (*kumbhakāraḥ*), and "city-builder" (*nagarakāraḥ*) are words ending in *kṛt* suffixes.
The occurrence of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) is tenfold, according to the distinction of the ten tenses and moods (*lakāra*).
Furthermore, it is twofold, by virtue of having as its domain either roots (*dhātu*) or nominal stems (*subdhātu*).
"He cooked" (*apākṣīt*), "he cooks" (*pacati*), and "he will cook" (*pakṣyati*) are examples of verbal forms derived from roots.
[The words] "apallavayat," "pallavayati," and "pallavayiṣyati" belong to the category of *saubdhātavīya* (words formed with the suffix *ṇic*).

Thus, this entire collection of words, consisting of five types, when combined with one another, leads to infinity. And from that arises this well-known saying among the learned: even if Bṛhaspati were the speaker and Śatakratu the student for a thousand divine years, there would still be no end to the mass of words.
