In this regard, there is a Vedic [text]:
"The Apsaras Urvaśī desired Purūravas, the son of Iḍā.
Regarding this matter—
From the Moon was born the venerable Budha; he begot Purūravas, the first of kings and the son of Iḍā.
And the Apsaras Smaravatī fell in love with him—what else need be said? For Urvaśī had already captivated the heart of Indra with her smile.
Or as it is said:

"That which shines as this orb is the Great Hymn (Mahaduktha), those are the *ṛcs*, that is the world of the *ṛcs*; and that which shines as this radiance is the Great Vow (Mahāvrata), those are the *sāmans*, that is the world of the *sāmans*; and that person who is in this orb is Agni, those..."
"The world of the Yajus is this very triple knowledge that shines.
Regarding this point:
"That orb which shines in the sky as the maker of day is the Ṛcs; those rays which gleam are the Sāmans; and this person within the orb, though minute, is the Yajus."

Thus, may that Sun—who is the essence of the three Vedas, who is the knower of the Vedas, who is the entire assembly of all things, and who is the source of both heaven and liberation, remaining unchanging—be for your glory.
And this is what they call the "stealing of the Veda": "Homage be to that sacred revelation (śruti), which they milk at every step."
"The sages, the authors of the scriptures, and the poets [have spoken] according to their own understanding."
The Smārta says:
"By one who has been charged with many matters and who denies them all,
but whose claim regarding even a single part is proven, that which he was accused of must be paid."
Regarding this matter:
"O Haṃsa, give me back my beloved; her whereabouts was taken away by you.
That which is sought must be returned when one part of the claim has been established."
The storytellers say: "That path by which Vālī went after being slain is not a narrow one;
abide in the proper time, O Sugrīva, and do not follow the path of Vālī."
In this regard:
"Having cast aside the pride obtained from a mere fragment of new sovereignty, let the former agreement be reconsidered.
Neither Bali, who was eager to devour the world, nor Antaka, whose hunger was never satiated, acted thus."
The Paurāṇikas say:
"Whichever direction the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu looked upon even with a smile,
the gods, bewildered by fear, offered salutation to that very direction."
In this regard:
"To that quarter where he, wandering through even the three worlds, took refuge by chance as the abode of Fortune—
there let the gods offer salutation at the three junctions of the day with their hands brushing against the jewels of their crowns."
On this point, they say:
"The study of the meanings of the Vedas with their auxiliary branches, the *Itihāsas*, and the *Purāṇas*,
as well as the practice of storytelling, is the one medicine for the art of poetry."
Like a true poet with eyes purified by the collyrium of discernment, one perceives even the most subtle meaning through the two eyes of Itihāsa and Purāṇa.
"Just as poets are praised for their composition on the meaning of the Vedas,
so too are those who compose upon the Smṛtis, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas."
The authority [of language] is twofold: that of the Mīmāṃsakas and that of the logicians (*tārkika*).
Among these, for the first [the Mīmāṃsakas], the universal (*sāmānya*) is the denotatum (*abhidheya*) of the word, while the particular (*viśeṣa*) is its referent (*artha*).
In this regard—
“Even a word denoting a universal, when it reaches me while being uttered, becomes fixed upon a specific object of denotation;
for when it is said, ‘A certain woman,’ my mind constantly takes as its object that very same one with the beautiful eyes.”
Among the systems of logic, the Sāṃkhya states: "The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being.
The limit of both these is seen by the seers of reality."
In this regard:
"Those who are performers of sacrifice whose fame is widespread, those who are rulers of the earth, these deer-eyed women for whom further talk of saṃsāra has ceased,
and these trees seen here bowed down with fruits and flowers— in the world, it is this venerable Earth alone that shines forth in such forms."

The proponent of the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika school raises the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "What kind of causal complex (*sāmagrī*) does that Lord possess as a creator? The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that He, possessing unsurpassed sovereignty, is the creator.
In this regard:
"What is his desire? What is his body? What indeed is his means? What is the support for the three worlds? What does the Creator create, and by what material cause?

Since you possess inconceivable sovereignty, this fallacious reasoning—ill-placed and out of its time, having stolen away the intellect—only makes certain people talkative to the delusion of the world."
Regarding the cognition [of the speaker]: words are preceded by the intention to speak; they should therefore indicate that very intention.
In this regard—

"Let it be known that words indicate the speaker's intended meaning, for when a lover forcibly kisses his beloved while she is full of passion, the speech 'No, no, no! Do not, do not, do not touch me!'—though intent on prohibition—becomes prescriptive once the knot of pride has loosened."
The materialist (laukāyatika) [claims]: consciousness arises from the elements, like the power of intoxication.
Regarding this—
“In this world, those who contemplate the witness declare it to be manifold and distinct from this body;
yet, O fair-toothed one, those very contemplators perish along with their contemplation.”
The Ārhata [maintains]:
the self is co-extensive with the body;
otherwise, there would be either the futility of the body or the futility of the self.
In this regard:
"Victorious are those who declare that the self is nothing more than the body;
for even from a kiss upon it, there has arisen this horripilation of mine over my entire frame."
Because poetic science (*kāvyavidyā*) is intended for all circles of assembly, he should examine these and other such matters for the sake of his proficiency.
And they say:
"Whatever matters are harsh with logic that a poet values in his compositions..."
Like the rays of the sun upon the moon, they radiate a certain splendor.

Regarding the *samayavidyās*, the Śaivasiddhāntin says: “May the Supreme Lord protect us— he who has transcended the terrible and the most terrible, who surpasses Brahmā, Vidya, and Kalā, and who pervades both the supreme and the non-supreme states.”
The *Pañcarātra* states:
“May the ancient seers, who are without beginning or end, subtle, vast, and the instructors [of all],—
may Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Vāsudeva dispel all my fevers.”
The Buddhist Siddhāntin says:
"May whatever defilements produced by the Kali age fall upon me; may that world be liberated!
Indeed, through my own good conduct, may all sentient beings proceed to the blissful realm of supreme happiness."
The same applies to other systems of tenets as well.

Within the three royal systems of tenets, there is one from the *Arthaśāstra*: “For a king who has provided for his governance through both tranquility (*śama*) and exertion (*vyāyāma*), [the enemy] says: ‘Bend your front foot high toward me; look at me while I stand thus.’”
“A kingdom full of many deceptions is not easy to manage for those who lack royal discipline; Fortune is difficult to propitiate and deceives one whose mind is not vigilant.”
From the *Nāṭyaśāstra*: “Hold the creeper-like arm thus, O Goddess; bend your limb thus; do not bow too high; curve the tips of your feet; look at me while I stand here.
May the clapping rhythms (tālikās) of Śambhu—drawn out by the breaking of the suspended tempo as he makes the Goddess dance with his own mouth-drum sounding like a rain-cloud—protect you all.”
From the *Kāmasūtra*:
"It is no wonder that Lakṣmī, having cast aside Viṣṇu, came to you;
for she is fond of the Mandara mountain, while you are one who delights in battle."
The worldly [friendship], however, is of two kinds: natural and cultivated. Of these, the first is as follows:
"O beloved, that bond of affection which we first formed was such that it remained even in the house of our adversary, as praiseworthy as the mending of a cracked pot."
“People say that we two must now dwell right here in this house; fie on the love of women for strangers, and fie on their long-lived existence!”
Or as it is said:
"The residue of sugarcane juice, of curd-whey, of curd, of flour-based preparations, and of boar's meat goes to Phālguna."
The second [type] is twofold: that produced by all people collectively and that produced by only a few people. Of these two, the first is of many kinds due to the multiplicity of regions.
Among those, the Southern type—
“Having tasted black pepper, the Dravidian women drink honey from mouths made bright with betel, as they take bites from the lips of their lovers.”
Or as it is said:
"Desist, O Madana! Who are you? O Caitra, what power does the moon have here? For its flower-arrows fall with blunted points.
These hearts of the beloveds of Kuntala are like the hard knots of scars from striking, possessing the essence of adamant."
The Northerner says:
"The Nepalese, adorned with moist musk, pass the summer nights together with their lovers upon beds of *granthiparṇaka* leaves."
The second verse:

"While the deer-eyed woman’s eye—its curved lashes slightly closing in a sidelong glance, tremulous like a wave upon the river of her long outer corner—was turned toward him, the circle of female friends rose with a pretext and departed, saying, ‘Who is this speaking? as they interrupted their husband’s playful conversation by whispering to one another."
A composition consists either of a narrative framework fashioned by a poet’s imagination or merely of its thematic content.
Of these, the first is exemplified by:
“There is a sovereign of the sword-wielding *vidyādharas* named Citraśikha.”
On the lap of the Malaya mountain to the south, in front of the city of Ratnavatī, was the lord.
Citrasundarī, the daughter of Ratnākara and the uterine sister of Queen Śrī, became his wife by choice during her svayaṃvara.
The second verse:

"That man who anoints the moonlight with sandalwood paste, he sprinkles the jasmine garland with perfumed water, and he makes honey sweet with molasses—he who proclaims the celebrated virtues of His Majesty Vīracūḍāmaṇi; and he too seeks the brilliance of pearls by means of a whetstone."
Regarding this, they say:
"He whose creative intuition does not fail even when composing verses that are devoid of meaning is the leader of the village of poets; the rest are merely his dependents."
That which is other than those already mentioned is the miscellaneous (*prakīrṇaka*).
Regarding this, the *Hastiśikṣīya* states:
"The necklace, having attained the state of a momentary laugh of the clouds, is scattered across the quarters; it strikes against the full breasts of the celestial damsels shimmering in the sky."
May that spray protect you—the spray driven by Airāvaṇa out of intoxication, like a fierce moon eclipsed, which steals away the beauty of the tawny ripened lavalī fruit.
The Gem-Examiner says:
"Two types of diamond color are prescribed by the wise for lords of the earth, but not for common people:
that which is as red as a broken piece of hibiscus or coral, or that which resembles the juice of turmeric."

The Dhanurvedīya says: "He saw the Self-born [Brahmā], who had his fist placed at the right corner of his eye, with shoulders bent and the left foot drawn back, holding his beautiful bow drawn into a circle, prepared to strike."
According to the Yogaśāstra:
"You are the single swan within the lotus-heart of all living beings; you are awake and you sleep, you perceive and yet you are not perceived.
By worshipping You, those of expansive intellect, having effected the severance of their bonds, become free from affliction and possess stainless splendor."
The same applies to other miscellaneous examples.
Regarding the union of the appropriate:
"This Pāṇḍya king has long necklaces draped over his shoulders, and his body is anointed with yellow sandalwood paste."
With its ridges reddened by the morning sun, it shines like the king of mountains with the outpouring of waterfalls.
The conjunction with the agent:
“While the celestial elephants, making the water of their ichor tasteless for the bees, caused a thousand-fold pain to the eyes of the Blessed One, the enemy of Namuci;
and while the waters of the heavenly river were turned to mud by the dust [raised by the army], the women of the celestial realm, dejected, lamented his addiction to such expeditions.”
An example of conjunction produced by creation (*utpādyasaṃyoga*):
“If two separate streams of the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā were to fall into the sky,
they might be compared to his chest, dark as a *tamāla* tree, adorned with a string of pearls.”
Metaphorical modification through conjunction (*saṃyogavikāra*): “By your fame, mingled with its affection for the virtues [of others] and spreading abroad,
half-a-patch of saffron has suddenly appeared upon the faces of the women who are the quarters.”
Or as it is said:
“The ocean goes mad, the night-lily bursts open, the day-lotuses contract, the moonstones ooze, and the *śephālikā* flowers fall away;
the *cakra* birds drink the water of the moonlight with throats gradually relaxed, while the moon, bearing a luster like camphor, becomes the crest-jewel of the sky.”
This, which is devoted to the origin of meanings, has been told to poets; for one who is confident in this field, there shall never be any distress regarding meaning.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Sixteen Methods of Poetic Meaning," in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) on the Instruction of Meaning within Rājaśekhara’s *Kāvyamīmāṃsā*, the Secret of the Poet.
Chapter Nine:
Instruction on Wealth (The Misappropriation of Wealth)
"It is threefold," says Drahuiṇi: divine, divine-human, and human.
"It is sixfold," says Yāyāvarīya: [including] that of the netherworld (pātālīya).
The mortal-pātālīya, the divine-pātālīya,
and the divine-mortal-pātālīya.
Regarding that, the celestial [verse] says:
"Remembering how Rambhā, while staying in her own quarters during the night, sang with a lute like Tumburu’s song— her voice faltering from the longing caused by separation from Nalakūvara—
the very Indra, deprived of sleep by Airāvaṇa’s flickering ears, was made to cast his gaze again in agitation upon the smiling face of Śacī."
The divine-human [drama] is of four kinds;
one variety consists of the descent of a divine being to the mortal world and the ascent of a mortal being to heaven.
The second [type] consists of a divine being in a mortal state and a mortal being in a divine state;
the third consists of the imaginative construction of a divine narrative.
The fourth [type of descent] is by means of manifesting a divine form through supernatural power (*prabhāva*).
Regarding that, the arrival of a divine being among mortals is as follows:
"The Lord of Śrī, the abode of the world, in order to govern the world, entered the glorious household of Vasudeva."
Immediately after the sight of spring, Hari [beheld] from the sky the sage born from the body of Hiraṇyagarbha.
The Departure of a Mortal to Heaven:
“O son of Pāṇḍu, this is the Nandana grove, where couples who lick the nectar of immortality sport with wines produced by mere thought, for which the wish-fulfilling trees provide the vessels.
Even here, the circular basins at the roots of the *santānaka* trees are filled without effort by the waters of clear cascades mingling with the moonlight.”
The descent of the divine into mortal state: "As that lineage of the Yadus thus flourished, Vasudeva was born, whose wife was Devakī;
what more need be said? And from him, Padmanābha came to be embraced by sixteen thousand women."

The divine state of a mortal: "O Goddess, mortals, standing on the edge of the bank with one foot placed upon a celestial vehicle and supporting themselves with their hands on pairs of golden staffs, gaze out of curiosity at their own bodies as they are tossed by your waves."
The invention of a fictional past (*divyetivṛttaparikalpanā*):
"On this sandy bank of the Sarayū, made bright by the spreading flood of moonlight, a game of dice was played for a long time by two perfected youths.
One says, 'Kaṃsa was the first slain'; the other says, 'Kaiṭabha'. You, tell the truth: which of them was killed by you there first?"
With his divine nature manifested through his power:
"O Earth, do not go to the netherworld! Why else do you tremble while being split asunder by this wicked demon?
O Goddess whose greatness is drunk by the feet of the Three Worlds, is it not because of your strength?"

"O Lord, the world is filled with You; even the foot of Your infant body is too large for the cradle"—as the Upholder of the World thus spoke while dreaming in his sleep, may Yaśodā protect you, her cheeks smiling as they bristled with joy at bowing before His feet marked with the wheel.
The mortal [observes]:

"The daughter-in-law functions in the place of the mother-in-law; the son occupies the station of the father at every step. One empty thing is replaced by another object; like the flow of a river's current, the world flows on full, its sequence of discernment unperceived and dense, and yet there is no returning."
The one from Pātāla says:
"Karkoṭaka bows ten million times before Takṣaka; grant him sight. Kapila and Kulika stand ready with palms joined in service to you. Svastika honors you.
This Padma, out of devotion, prostrates himself before you. Here is Kambala, and here is Bala; let this king of serpents go to his own home with his attendants, and let Śaṅkhapāla be sent forth."
The mortal-infernal [verse]: "O Ārdrāvala, go! You do not know how to draw back the ear;
the disciple of Hara’s disciple draws the bow twice but does not fix the arrow."
Therefore, behold now with curiosity how the mortal [Arjuna] strikes down even the crown of Kiritin (Indra) with his arrows.
Here too, as before, there is a following of the distinctions between the pure, the mixed, and the dark; [as in the example] concerning the celestial and subterranean realms:
“May he protect you, whose body-stalk has the crest-jewel as its pericarp, and the collection of hoods as its leaves.”
"The lotus of the ear-serpent of the wielder of the Pināka shines forth, with its flickering tongue as its filaments."
Belonging to heaven, earth, and the netherworld:
"There was the sage Āstīka, who caused wonder by protecting Takṣaka and the lineage of the hooded serpents from the sacrifice of the son of Parīkṣit, as well as that of Indra;
even today, his fame is sung with graceful movements by the throngs of serpent-wives as they sportfully sway the sandalwood creepers on the Malaya mountain."
"The teachers [say]: 'This very thing, when delineated in this manner and utilized, becomes an inexhaustible treasury of meaning. [Objection:
'Granted that it is an inexhaustible treasury of meaning;
however, it is of two kinds: that which is well-established upon investigation and that which is charming only so long as it is not investigated.'"
"The treatises (*śāstra*) are based on those two [the Veda] first, and the poetic works (*kāvya*) follow after them"—so say the followers of Udbhaṭa.
For example:
"Making the sky tawny with its radiance as it crossed the mass of waters..."
Hanūmat, possessing the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, leapt up into the sky.
Or for example:
"Having ascended into the sky, dark as a sword,
those supreme seers reached the mountain peak of Oṣadhiprastha with minds possessing equal speed."
And as it is said: "That very water of the rivers becomes a great mass of flames through its heat," and so forth.
“This form of space, or of water and so forth, is not based on its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpanibandhana*), but rather is based on appearance (*pratibhāsanibandhana*).
And appearance does not abide in the object as being identical to it;

for if that were the case, then the orbs of the sun and moon—which are perceived by sight to have a measurement of twelve *aṅgulas*—would not exist as the mere circle of the earth described in the Purāṇas and other traditional scriptures,” says Yāyāvarīya.
In this way, [the same applies] to the stars and so forth, to rivers, waters, and other things.
Furthermore, the actual nature of an object as it appears is useful for composition in both technical treatises (*śāstra*) and poetry (*kāvya*).
As an example in a treatise:
“In the cloudless, pure waters of the sky, where the stars were like blooming water-lilies, the lord of the constellations appeared like a swan.”
Furthermore, these poetic works consist of nothing but this [sentiment].
Āparājiti says: "Granted that the caravan of meanings is indeed boundless; however, composition is appropriate only for that which possesses rasa, not for that which is devoid of rasa."
As it has been said:

"In this context, one should not compose sentences concerning liquor, flowers, women, twilight, the rising of the moon, and so forth— even if they are elegant— either too frequently or if they do not accord with the prevailing sentiment."
However, that effort which consists in the description of rivers, mountains, oceans, cities, horses, chariots, and so forth,
and which results merely in proclaiming the poet's power, is not approved here by those of expanded intellect.
"Yes," says Yāyāvarīya.
"There certainly exists an object that is experienced as being either conducive to or detrimental to rasa;
however, in poetry, it is the words of the poet that flavor or render flavorless, not the objects themselves."
This is perceived through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).
In that regard, the possession of color, form, and taste like a river is [illustrated by]:
"O slender-waisted one, behold this Tāmraparṇī as it pours into the ocean, its waters drawn up by the opened shells of oysters."
“Whose waters transform themselves into the form of necklaces upon the swelling breasts of fair-browed women.”

The quality of having rasa (sentiment) consisting of the description of mountains: “Those are the banks of the rivers near the Malaya mountains, the haunts of deer-eyed women, and the beloved dwelling-place for the practice of archery of the blessed God of Love;
where, during nights dark with moonlight, female cakora birds—having swallowed the darkness—drink the pearl-like moonbeams with their beaks upturned and their throats quivering.”
The ocean’s charming behavior consists in this:
that wine makes the "deer-eyed" women take on the singular importance of amorous agitation (*kilakiñcita*); that the moonlit sky brings about the distress of the anger between couples;
that youth is the eternal friend of the gods in heaven; and that Lakṣmī is the presiding deity of all prosperity.
In this way, there is also the quality of aesthetic flavor (*rasavattā*) in the description of the city, the horse, and so forth.
Even in the context of separation (*vipralambha*), there is an abundance of flavor:

"Entities are of different natures; because they function by being superimposed upon that [object], they do not lead to stability. Others, though possessing similar forms, have their excellent aesthetic flavors rendered fruitless by the thwarted longing [of the lover]."
Therefore, it attached itself at will to the former [objects], while being repelled by others; for how could this heart of my beloved, once diminished, find delight elsewhere?
A bad poet excludes aesthetic flavor even in a case of deception;
let there be flavor in real things or not, it resides in the speech of the poet.
“Whether the form of an object be this way or that,
its aesthetic flavor (rasavattā) depends upon the particular nature of the speaker;
thus, that which one who is impassioned praises, another who is dispassionate censures, while one who is neutral remains indifferent toward it”— so says Pālyakīrti.
“For those with whom the night passes like a moment together with their beloved, the moon is exceedingly cold; for those separated from their lovers, it causes torment like a firebrand.
But for us, there is neither beloved nor separation; thus, for those deprived of both, this moon shines with the form of a mirror—neither hot nor cold.”
“The nature of a thing is not of a fixed essence, but is to be conveyed through the various turns of expression of a clever poet,” says Avantīsundarī.
Thus she states:
“In poetry, where the poet is not subject to external constraints, the nature of the object and its merits or defects depend upon the power of the expression.”
"Praising him, he binds the immortal-rayed moon; yet the rogue calls that very same moon a 'defiler' (nindu) because it is the source of faults (doṣākara)."
“Both are valid,” says Yāyāvarīya;
moreover, it is of two kinds,
by way of being the subject matter of either detached verses or continuous compositions.
Each of those two is also fivefold:
the pure (*śuddha*), the variegated (*citra*),
and that arising from a story (*kathottha*).
It is the ground for dramatic construction and possesses narrative elements;
therein, that which is devoid of past events is the pure [drama].
That same [drama] is manifold when accompanied by elaboration (*saprapañca*); it is classified as having a real historical basis (*vṛttetivṛtta*), arising from a story (*kathottha*),
based on a probable historical account (*sambhāvitetivṛtta*), or originating from an invented plot (*saṃvidhānakabhū*).
That which possesses an invented plot is the *ākhyāyikā*.
Among these,
the *muktaka* is the pure [verse].

“When her husband commits his first offense, that young woman— without any instruction or reproach, yet with her limbs turning in graceful agitation and her speech taking a winding, variegated course—
merely weeps, her lotus-eyes cast down, as tears fall from the very roots of her bright cheeks, rolling and shimmering like water.”
Citra says:

“When her lover has arrived from afar, the eyes of the proud woman are expectant; when he speaks, they widen; when he embraces her, they turn crimson; when he takes hold of her garment, the surface of her brow is arched with anger.
But when there is the act of bowing at her feet, oh, how the eye—filled with a flood of tears—becomes in an instant so skilled in manifold expression toward the one who has committed an offense!”
Kathottha says:
"Because King Śrīśarmagupta, having given the goddess Dhruvasvāminī to the Lord of the Sky (Śiva), returned with his boldness shattered,
it is there on that very Himālaya— where kinnaras warble in the corners of the great caves— that the glories of the women of your city, O Kārttikeya, are sung by throngs."
The Stage of the Plot:

"Having seen her two beloveds seated together on a single seat, the rogue approaches from behind with respect; under the pretext of engaging in a playful sport, he closes the eyes of one while his neck is slightly bent, his hair standing on end, and his cheeks glistening with suppressed laughter as he kisses the other, whose heart overflows with love."
And as it is said:
"When, my body stained tawny by saffron water from the bathing place, I mistook that royal female swan for a *cakravākī* and separated her from her mate—the male play-swans;
the fruit of that sin of mine now ripens in that we, though bound by love, dwell together in one city, yet, O beloved, there is not even the proximity of our eyes."
The narrator says: "The benefactor born of the Haihaya lineage, using the tusks first fashioned from the wild elephants brought for the sake of those who sought his aid, built a temple for Śambhu."
In the *Nibandha*, it is stated as follows:

“I became for a long time the recipient of glances— glances that were steady yet expanding, with creeper-like brows quivering, smooth yet slightly closed, possessing a wide outer fringe, and somewhat contracted upon falling upon each other’s eyes.”
Citra:

"By the side-long glances of that long-lashed-eyed maiden—glances languid, rolling, innocent, tender, motionless, and slow; glances whose pupils were bright with a smile of inner wonder expanding all the more—my defenseless heart has been stolen, cast down, drunk up, and awakened."
The story begins: "The Lord of Creatures, his senses aroused by desire, set his heart upon his own daughter;
then, having suppressed that agitation, he experienced this consequence."
The locus of the narrative:
"O Lord, withdraw your anger, withdraw it!"— while these words were still traveling through the air by the mouths of the gods,
that fire born from the eye of Bhava reduced Madana to nothing but ashes."
The *ākhyānakavat* (containing a narrative): "‘Touch the crescent moon on your husband’s head with this,’ said a friend jokingly.
Having colored her feet, she [Sītā], having offered a blessing, struck her back wordlessly with a garland."
Furthermore,
one should be attentive toward all languages— just as with the Sanskrit— one according to one's ability, according to one's inclination, and according to one's interest.
And one should understand the proficiency of the functions of signifier and signified between word and meaning.
As it has been said:

"One meaning is expressed in Sanskrit, another is composed by a skillful poet in Prākṛta; in this [work], another is in Apabhraṃśa speeches, and what more can be said? Another follows the sequence of the Bhūtabhāṣā."
Some may discern [the truth] with two or three words, and another perhaps with four; but for that great poet whose intellect has attained such discernment, his fame bathes the worlds.
For a poet whose mind is refined by such dense expressions,
his eloquence shall not falter even on a path that is difficult to traverse.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, "The Expansion of Meaning," within the section on the Instruction of Meaning, in the first book, the Secret of the Poet, of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.
Chapter 10:

A mouth with betel,

"Fine flowers for the head":
they declare that the cultivation of pure conduct is the means of winning over Sarasvatī;

It is a common saying that a painting takes on the very form of the artist; likewise,

He avoids seeking out secrets from all sides, turns away from looking at the poetry of others, and speaks truthfully regarding both what has not been said and what has been said.
His residence is well-swept and clean.
It contained various locations suited for each of the six seasons,
featured groves of trees with many roots fashioned as resting places,

It possessed lotus ponds with long steps,

In the absence of him, at the Atirātra and other sacrifices, one of the names previously mentioned is used.

"For utterances that have shifted to another meaning are not recognized [as their original], yet they are pleasing; however, for their sake, there may be 'takings' even from what has already been taken," so says Yāyāvarīya.
“There is no poet who is not a thief, nor is there any merchant who is not a thief;
he alone rejoices without reproach who knows how to conceal [what he has taken].”
One is a creator-poet, another is a transformer,
yet another is a concealer, and still another is a collector.
"He who perceives something new here in the expression of words and meanings, and sketches something from the ancients, let him be considered a great poet."
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, "The Appropriation of Words," in the first section, "The Secrets of the Poet," of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.

The classifications of poets,
and an examination of the conceptualization of the reflected image:
"On the path trodden by ancient poets, an untouched subject matter is difficult to find."
"Therefore, one should strive to refine that very [speech]," so say the teachers.
"No," says Vākpatirāja:
"Though its essence has been extracted day by day by noble poets throughout the duration of cyclic existence..."
Even now, the flow of his words shines forth with its seal unbroken.”
And one should apply oneself to other treatises in order for that [meaning] to appear therein;
for some say, "In the immersion into that, meanings which share a single source manifest individually," while others say,
"The fruit is the transformation by means of the reflection of the meanings contained therein."
"For the cognitions of great souls are in agreement and present a single object; therefore, one should not disregard them for fear of abandoning that [truth]," so say some.
"No," says Yāyāvarīya.
The Sarasvatī eye discerns for itself the multitude of objects—both seen and unseen—through a meditative concentration that transcends the range of speech and mind.
Regarding this, they say:
"Even for the great poet Sūtpa, it is Sarasvatī who reveals both word and meaning."
For another person, even though awake, the eye is blind regarding that [object];
for great poets are like those born blind regarding an object never before seen by others, yet they possess divine vision regarding its opposite.
It is not something that the three-eyed god or the thousand-eyed one perceive, which poets see even with their physical eyes.
In the mirror of the intoxicated [vision] of poets, the universe is reflected.
"How indeed shall we be seen?"—with such a competitive urge for precedence (*ahampūrvikā*), words and meanings run forward before the great-souled ones.
That which yogis see through perfected meditative concentration, [is here revealed].
Regarding this, there are infinite eloquent sayings among the great poets, such as: "The wise roam therein with speech.
And Yāyāvarīya says: "We have studied the entire meaning, yet we have mastered only that which lies within the three paths."
Namely: that which has another source, that which has a concealed source, and that which is sourceless.
Among these, that which has another source is twofold: resembling a reflection and resembling a painting.

Those who have concealed their place of birth are also of two kinds: those equal to ordinary embodied beings and those resembling those who enter the bodies of others. Those who are without a [physical] womb are of only one kind.
Among these—
That poetry in which the entire meaning remains the same while there is merely the composition of different sentences would be a semblance of a reflection, lacking ultimate distinction.
For example:
"May those serpents, dark as bees, shimmering upon the region of Paśupati’s throat, protect you—
those by which the Kālakūṭa poison shines as if with sprouts grown through the pleasure of being sprinkled with drops of water from the nectar of the moon."
And as it is said:
"Victorious are the great serpents blue upon the throat of the Blue-throated One,
appearing like sprouts of the Kālakūṭa poison drenched by the flowing waters of the Gaṅgā."
To what extent? That poetry in which an object appears as if divided by the act of poetic embellishment is called "resembling a painting" by those skilled in the meaning [of poetry].
Regarding that very same meaning, for example:
"Victorious are the white serpents hanging from Śambhu’s matted locks,
appearing like sprouts of the moon-root drenched by the flowing waters of the Gaṅgā."
When there is a cognition of non-difference despite the difference of the object due to extreme similarity,
even wise poets compose poetry that treats similar bodies as identical.
For example:
"From the state of a sheep onwards, until one reaches the horse as the ultimate limit, a beast that lives happily is truly fortunate.
Was their creation brought about by some scorched elephant, or perhaps by a forest, or else by the palace of a king—that which serves as their refuge?"
Regarding this point:

"In every house, the stones are of a single kind; because they are used as common tools, they are both offered and honored. But the splendor of those precious gems shines forth, for their dwelling is either in the palace of a sovereign or within their own mine."

That poem in which there is a single unity of the root theme, yet an extensive and manifold arrangement of its accessories, is comparable to the "entry into another's body" (parapurapraveśa) and is to be contemplated by skilled poets.
For example:
"When his enemies' wives, seeing from all sides the sky during the rainy season filled with masses of vast clouds surpassed by his thundering roars,

repeatedly inhaled the breezes from the *kadamba* trees— with tears of joy clearly manifest due to the fear of an impetuous military expedition abandoned [by their husbands]— their eyes slightly contracted."
Regarding this matter:
"Having plucked a fresh kadamba flower from her beloved— the very sign of the approaching rainy season that portends the end of his expeditions— his enemies' wives,
filled with joy, kissed it, placed it upon their eyes, set it upon their hearts, somehow fixed it in the parting of their hair, and finally made it an ear-ornament."
These four foundations give rise to the thirty-two methods of poetic composition for poets.
Among these subjects, there are four types of poets whose names correspond to their functions—like magnets—and a fifth, who perceives objects never before seen.
As they say:
“The magnet that causes wandering, the one that attracts, and that which draws and melts—such is the worldly poet; but the other is the supramundane wish-fulfilling gem.”
That poet who, while describing even an ancient subject, causes it to appear as if it were unprecedented through such means as novelty and so forth, would be a deluder.
He who kisses another’s meaning with his own captivating speech, imparting a fresh luster even to a slight suggestion— he is considered a "kisser" poet.
He who draws in the meaning of another's speech and establishes it within his own words by means of some clever artifice is remembered as a "poet-thief" (karṣaka-kavi).
He who, by making [the meaning] unrecognizable, brings novelty to his own statement—
even while dissolving the root meaning— is a true poet.
"He from whom a multitude of objects with diverse forms arises, born solely from his aesthetic sentiment and equal to his own thought—
a sight never before seen even by the most skillful ancients— is that peerless poet, a wish-fulfilling gem."
And its meaning is expressed by words;
that [meaning] is threefold, through the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane, and by their combination.
The worldly example:

"O silkworm-creeper, do not harbor pride in your color; what is the use of your transient floral display? Let this single stalk of sugar-cane from Puṇḍra shine forth, for it exudes its juice even without the application of a machine."
The extraordinary (alaukika):

“The Goddess has given birth to a son! Dancers, O Gaṇas, why do you stand still? Thus spoke Bhṛṅgiriṭi with uplifted arms; and as he was embraced by Cāmuṇḍā, whose voice was stolen away by joy, may the sound produced by the impact of their mutual embrace—arising from the cracking of old, massive bones—protect you, a sound that surpasses the deep resonance of the drums of the gods.
Miśra:
“O Lord, as long as you remain within your mother’s womb, filling it with your mass of light, may the falls of the breaths from your mother— emitting the pollen of the lotus of your navel—
be daily the destruction of your sins, as they are received joyfully by Balarāma, who has formed a circle of hoods.”
And regarding those four subjects—
these four subjects which I myself have declared in the instruction on the appropriation [of themes] by poets—
become thirty-two when followed by their respective divisions.
In that regard, there are conceptual constructions resembling reflections;
that very same object is fragmented by the inversion of its preceding and succeeding parts,
as follows:

“Having seen another elephant and feeling a desire to tear it apart, the king of elephants went sniffing at the driver’s words, regarding them as mere straw; out of love for his mate, there is no bond for a living being equal to that.”
Regarding this point:
"For even a creature whose mind is devoid of discernment possesses a bond of affection that is like an unchained fetter;
for against every rival elephant toward whom he set out, the lordly elephant was long held back by his mate."

A *khaṇḍa* (section) is the presentation of half of a large subject matter. “First, the jujube fruit in the forest becomes mostly pale; thereafter, it assumes a brownish hue; then, its body is suffused with the quality of redness due to the excess of ripening; and finally, as it slowly begins to dry, its form becomes uneven due to its own protruding ridges, and it loses its fragrance—thus it attains the state of being mere sapless pulp.”
Regarding this point:

"In this forest, the jujube fruit bears a state of bitterness because its own body— perfected through long acquaintance with the process of ripening— has increased its ruddy quality, thereby nourishing a parched condition that causes its surface to become cracked and uneven."
In brief and in detail, it is like a drop of oil;
as it is said:
"By the weight of whose body pressing down, [the earth] goes toward the depths of the netherworld..."
The Earth once again remembered the tusk of Mahāvarāha.
In this regard:

"When her husband, the Lord of the Serpents, grew weary as he struggled beneath the weight of the vast jeweled slabs of the mountain, sinking under their pressure, the Earth— whose boundaries were marked by the shifting mass of great, unmoving pillars—
suddenly recalled the fierce tip of her fang, white from being ground upon the whetstone of the rows of massive bones on Hiraṇyākṣa’s chest, and shining with the brilliance of the full moon."
The "actor's costume" (*naṭanepathya*) refers to the translation of a composition written in one language into another language.
For example:
"No one who is suspicious of her husband desires [him], even if he is given by the wife of a traveler."
"Having seen the alms-food held between the middle of the bracelets that have slipped down onto her crossed hands."
“Suspicious of a snare, the crow does not wish to eat the morsel offered by the housewife of the traveler,
even though it rests in the middle of a bangle that has repeatedly slipped from her palm.”
Regarding this matter:

"The crow does not eat this offered rice-ball, though its cheeks are washed by the cleansing of tears; for, at the edge of the door, out of a lingering hope for union with her, it keeps its neck curved, its head bobbing, its eyes glancing sideways, fearing the snare."
*Chandovinimaya* (the exchange of meters) is the transposition of a meter.
For example:

“Kānte talpamupāgate vigalitā nīvī svayaṃ bandhanāt, tadvāsaḥ ślathamekhalāguṇadhṛtaṃ kiñcinnitambe sthitam. [When her beloved ascended the bed, the knot of her garment loosened of its own accord; her dress, held only by the slackened cord of her girdle, remained slightly upon her hips.]
"O friend, this much alone do I know; but as for his embrace, I have not even the slightest memory of who he was, who I was, what the pleasure was, or how it occurred."
Regarding this point:
"Blessed indeed are those women who, even during the intervals of lovemaking with their beloveds, can utter hundreds of confident and flattering words;
but as for me, O friends, I swear that when my lover's hand is placed upon the knot of my garment, I do not remember anything at all."
The reversal of the cause results in a change in the logical reason (*hetu*). For example:
"Then the moon, its luster dimmed by the movement of the dawn..."
It steals away the pallor from the cheeks of women whose desire has been withered by passion.
Regarding this point:
"Equal to the flower-bowed god [Kāma], and pale like the cheek of a pregnant woman,
the moon has placed its foot upon the summit of the mountain of sunrise."
*Saṅkrāntaka* (transference) is the transference of a perceived object to another [subject]. For example:
"Now, the weight of the hips, having become intimately acquainted with the sprouts of the tresses—those locks which are wet from bathing and wavering as they are loosened from their binding—"
Do even these swans, standing with necks outstretched, drink from the rows of water droplets falling through the sky from these [clouds] as they fly? O lady with eyes like blue lotuses!
Regarding this point:

"The droplets of water trickling from the tips of the matted locks of ascetics who have just bathed, muttered prayers, and performed austerities are drunk by fawns looking upward, distressed by the pain of thirst.
And a bird, agitated, protects its beloved—who is languid with the weight of love and whose mouth is suddenly drying—by embracing her and creating shade with the hollow of its wings."
The *sampuṭa* (casket) consists of the inclusion of the meanings of both sentences. For example:
“O fair-browed one, this is that Narmadā river which flows around the Vindhya mountain; she is known as the first wife of the Lord of Waters in the west.”
In whose midst you, with eyes agitated by the laughter of fear at the darting fish, were somehow brought slowly, very slowly, to the bank by me.”
For example:

"The waters of the Revā, filled with the warbling cries of peacocks as they are captivated by the sweet, gurgling sounds produced by the moving ripples entering the hollows of the navel-caves, are incessantly seized by Lāṭa women during their afternoon immersions."
Regarding this matter:

"During his campaigns for world conquest, he entered the rivers in every direction with his women, who—terrified by the laughter arising from the fear of being struck by schools of large fish—had their thighs trembling as they leaned against him; while the rivers’ waters, agitated by the repeated plunging into and emerging from the deep hollows of their navels, produced charming sounds that startled the quacking of the wild cocks."
Therefore, this [borrowed material], which robs a poet of his originality and is in every respect like a mere reflection, must be avoided;
for it has been said:
"They do not perceive as distinct a work situated within another poem."
They do not perceive their own bodies reflected [in it] as something separate.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, concerning the means of appropriating words and meanings and the classification of poets, including an examination of the "reflection-like" (pratibimbakalpa) variety of imitation, in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) on the secrets of the poet, within the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.

Chapter Thirteen: Conduct of Kings (Rājacaryā) The varieties of embezzlement of wealth, such as "resembling a painting" (ālekhyaprakhya) and others; the enumeration of those resembling a painting; the similar practice, and the equal progression.
For example:

"In the eight-pillared chamber, the orb of the sun, the lord of light, shone without blemish like a single cheek of Varuṇa’s beloved as she lay somewhat unconfined on her side, smeared with saffron paste. (1)
And as it is said:

"Behold, O beautiful one, the moon, having assumed the glow of its rising, attains a likeness to her face whose surface of cheeks is ruddy with saffron, as she shines forth every moment in the eastern direction."
The "removal of ornaments" (*vibhūṣaṇamoṣa*) refers to describing something as unadorned when it is actually adorned. For example:
"At its base it is dark like a blue water-lily; then, indeed, at its tip it is yellow like the ripening of a mango, resembling the sprout of the young moon."
With its crest smoky-grey from the fresh radiance of the sun, the flame of the lamp shone forth, manifesting a variety of transformations.
Regarding this point:
“At its base it is slightly blue; thereafter, a brownish glow appears in its center; then it becomes pale white, followed by a small flickering streak of red at the tip;
and finally, a mass of smoke-grey at the crest—thus, in an instant, the lamp’s flame, assuming a succession of various colors, shatters even the most densely gathered darkness.”
*Vyutkrama* (inversion) is the statement of a meaning that has been set forth in a particular sequence in a manner contrary to that sequence.
As in that very same [text]:
“Dark at the region of the crest, slightly reddish below that, and even lower than that, with a pale-white mass.”
Then, at its base, the flame of the lamp, tawny in hue, dispels the dense mass of blinding darkness.
*Viśeṣokti* (Poetic Peculiarization) is the mention of a particular when a general condition has been established.
For example:
“When the moon had thus risen, [the women], whose minds and eyes were stirred by the charming conversations of their beloved messengers...”
The women adopted a mode of adornment that was a perverse arrangement of ornaments, which caused their friends to laugh.
Regarding this matter:

"A certain woman, having sent forth her mental state toward her beloved, placed her girdle upon the slope of her breasts marked with white sandalwood paste, and fastened a necklace upon the curve of her hips."
An *uttaṃsa* (crest-jewel) occurs when a subordinate meaning attains prominence,
as for example:
“Then, illuminating the sky with masses of rays, [the sun] fair as a breast reddened by saffron...”
The moon slowly emerged from the eastern ocean like a golden pitcher.
Regarding this point:
"Then, as the dark cloth-garment was being torn apart, something was seen within—
the entire [disc] of the moon, beautiful with the saffron remaining on the breasts of the young night."
The "actor's costume" (naṭanepathya) refers to when that very same object is rendered otherwise through the power of verbal expression;
for example:
"That tilaka which was affectionately applied to the cheek—the moon of the face marked by the hare—[is now seen as something else]."
When her beloved broke the appointed time, the tremulous-eyed woman washed it away with tears from her eyes.
Regarding this matter:
"The leafy creepers, having been watered on the cheeks of playful women by tears of grief shed during the day,
became short-lived as they withered while the lovers were delaying."
"Even though the accompaniment (*parikara*) is identical, because the object of that accompaniment (*parikārya*) is otherwise, it is 'one with a single object of accompaniment' (*ekaparikārya*).
May he whose face is like the king of elephants protect these three worlds— he by whom, with his great trunk raised into the sky,
acting as the stalk for the lotus-plant that is the orb of the sun, the sprout-like tusk was bitten at its root.
Regarding this point:
"Victorious is the trunk-stalk of the elephant-bodied Lord, whose trunk is as straight as a reed;
for upon it, which serves as the ground for the root, the stalk, and the rhizome, there exists only a single tusk."
Pratyāpatti (restoration) is the return of a thing to its original state after it has undergone modification.
For example:
"The moon, whose orb was shrouded by frost, having regained its beauty through the sun's conjunction..."
Like a mirror blinded by breath, the moon does not shine.”
Regarding this point:
"Because of the departure of that dejection caused by its opposite, her face immediately shone forth,
clear as a mirror regains its own natural clarity when the mist of breath-vapor has vanished."
These are the varieties of that which resembles a painting; this is the path to be cultivated. And they say:
“Thus, this entire expansion of entities, through the variety of verbal expression,
attains a state of seeming diversity, like an actor assuming various roles by means of his makeup.”
Now, regarding the divisions of that which is equal to its own body:
the transformation of the object (*viṣayaparivṛtti*) is the assumption of another form through the application of that very same entity to a different object.
For example:

“May the breaths from the right nostril of Sthāṇu protect you—those breaths whose dust consists of the ashes on his parted body; those which are hostile to the fire-pot (the digestive heat); those licked by the serpent residing in his ear; and those which counteract the coolness of the moon; breaths that bear witness to the mental anguish of Śiva, whose body was divided by the enraged Daughter of the Mountain.”
In this regard:

"May the long, steady breaths of Hari protect you—those breaths which witnessed the memory of Rādhā; whose lotus-stalk nectar was drunk by the snakes upon his chest that had been withered by the heat [of his sighs]; and which were heard by Lakṣmī with envy as he suffered from the intense inner fever."
The "severance of a pair" (*dvandvavicchitti*) consists in the adoption of one form from between two forms of a thing.
For example:

"May that hair-braid of the enemy of the flower-arrowed god (Śiva) wipe away your affliction—[the hair-braid] which, upon seeing Indra, became agitated out of childishness by the weight of the waters of the Gaṅgā. In this verse, the word *keśabandhaḥ* ("hair-braid") is used to denote both the hair-braid itself and the serpent Śeṣa; by adopting the former form, the latter is excluded, thus effecting the "severance of the pair."

And there is the enemy of Krauñca (the peacock), whose beauty has eyes rolling in the delusion of the tiny fish darting in the thick spray; and the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa), gleaming with the joy of suddenly grasping a lotus stalk.
Regarding this matter:

"May the digit of the moon, shining like a fragment of moonlight upon the river that is the crest-tuft of Śiva, grant happiness—that digit which, due to its shimmering in the water, is suddenly seen and lost;
and which the serpent, mistaking it for a darting fish, repeatedly attempts to seize by contracting and extending his hood, only to become bewildered as he tries to close his hoods into a bud."
The *ratnamālā* (jewel-garland) is the interweaving of one meaning with other meanings, as in the following example:
“A cat licks its paws on its cheek, thinking them to be milk; an elephant grasps the moonbeams passing through the gaps in the trees, thinking them to be lotus stalks.”
"Even a woman steals the garment of one lying on the bed at the end of lovemaking"—oh, the moon, intoxicated by its own radiance, causes this entire world to wander in delusion!
In this regard:

"The moonlight was repeatedly swallowed by royal swans in their bowls, mistaking it for milk; it was gathered on the shoulders of beautiful women in their eagerness to smear themselves with camphor powder;

it was spread out by men from between their breasts, thinking it to be a silken garment during the confusion of lovers' privacy; and it was quickly licked by bees greedy for fresh Sindhuvara blossoms."
The mention of number (*saṅkhyollekha*) is the presentation of a meaning through a discrepancy in number.
For example:
"The nails on [Viṣṇu’s] feet are streaked by the reflections of the prostrating Nārāyaṇa."
"O Rudra, the ten Rudras serve you, just as the lunar mansions serve the moon."
In this regard:

"May that Blue-Throated One (Śiva) grant you joy— he at whose union with Umā’s single lotus-foot, upon which a toenail gleams, the moon, as if guilty of an offense, assumes as it were a sixfold nature."
A *cūlikā* (appendix) is the presentation of something additional after stating what is common [to both sides].
It is of two kinds: consistent (*saṃvādinī*) and inconsistent (*visaṃvādinī*). Of these, the first is as follows:
“Seeing the royal swan in the courtyard— anointed as if with moonbeams, resembling a cluster of moon-rays, and like a beautiful lotus— the timid female swan cries out with a voice choked by tears.”
Regarding this point:

"On the palace roof, shimmering with the spreading radiance of the moonlight, the royal swan of the house did not perceive his wife, whose wings were difficult to discern in the darkness; for his dull hearing was deceived by the jangling sound of her anklets, even though she was speaking right before him."
The second [type of *arthāntaranyāsa*] occurs in that same context, as follows:
“On the palace roof, bathed in moonlight and beautiful with heaps of pure pearls,
the female swan somehow perceived her mate by means of cries made resonant by the rhythmic clinking of her anklets.”
The connection of a prohibition with an injunction constitutes the removal of that injunction.
For example:
"O *kurabaka* tree, you are deprived of the pleasure of being struck by breasts; O *bakula* shrub, you must remember the sprinkling of the wine from [her] mouth."
"O Ashoka tree, you shall become full of grief because you are devoid of the touch of her feet"—thus did the wives of his enemies speak when he abandoned his own city.
Regarding this point:
"By means of the wine of their smiles, the planting of their feet, and their playful glances, the bakula shrub, the red aśoka tree,

and the tilaka tree were instantly made to undergo a great festival of blossoming by the women of that [city] as they successively conquered the regions of the directions— the shores of the ocean and the wildernesses."
The gathering together of many meanings in one place is a "cluster of rubies" (*māṇikyapuñja*).
For example:
"Under the guise of a mountain, the Earth-bride has extended her own long arm."
The Night, like a female friend, seems to apply the moon as a tilaka-mark upon his face.
And as it is said:

"Seeing the lion-moon standing upon the peak of the mountain of sunrise— beautiful with clusters of blossoming *atimuktaka* flowers and possessing rays for its bristling mane— the masses of the irresistible elephants of darkness immediately scattered."
And as it is said:
"The moon, with its mass of shimmering rays, marked by the spot, was set aside by the woman Night like a silver pitcher holding a blue lotus, intended for the consecration of the God of Love."
And as it is said:
"Behold, O slender-waisted one, the moon rises, breaking through the darkness with its milk-white rays."
"This is the beloved of Rohiṇī, the crest-jewel of the mountain of sunrise."
And as it is said:
"The moon rises, white as a lump of fresh butter, striking the beds of night-lotuses with the tips of its rays;
it is the loud laughter of the crystal slope of the Eastern Mountain, and the mirror for the face of the Night-bride."
And as it is said:
"In this lake of the sky, which smiles with the lilies of the stars, Madana bathed as if in waters of darkness, while the single moon-swan was departing."
In this regard:

"The moon rises in the lake of the sky, as if mocking the grace of a swan— the tilaka-mark of the saffron on the forehead of the city's matrons, the lion for the herd of elephants that is darkness, the silver consecration-vessel of the flower-armed Lord of the Earth, the unique crest-jewel of the Eastern Mountain, and a fresh mirror for the quarters."
The "kanda" (root) is so called because the primary meaning is expressed through specific particulars that emerge like shoots from it.
As it is said:
"It spreads forth at the openings of the streets and seems to cluster together upon the pinnacles of the palaces."
The moonlight, streaming forth from the vessel of the moon, blooms in the beds of night-lotuses.
Regarding this matter:
"The moonlight seems to glide through the sky, multiply among the night-lotuses, reflect upon the cheeks that resemble the stalks of withered reeds,
blossom in the waters, shimmer in the dwellings white with plaster, flutter upon the sprout-like folds of banner-cloths, and dance in the wind."
The moon is like a jar made of crystal, and its spot is like a lid upon it;
for from it flows forth the moonlight for a long time, like a stream of camphor powder.
The moon, like a white jeweled pitcher, with its deer-mark serving as a green grass cover,
sprinkles the courtyard of the sky with the waters of its moonlight, which fall like drops from that vessel.

The moon, with its flood of shimmering rays and marked by the sign of the hare, was set aside for the purpose of performing his consecration, like a silver pitcher adorned with a blue lotus by the lady Night.
"These are the enumerations for one who is equal to those with equal bodies;
this is the path of the 'Ullekhavat' (the one possessing the description), which is to be favored," said Surānanda.
Thus he spoke:
Victorious is that goddess Sarasvatī, the Veda herself, the source of well-being for poets;
she brings about a state of priceless worth through her own stylistic turns, by depicting whatever object of meaning is found here.
Now,
*huṇḍayuddha* is the logical transformation of a subject matter that has been presented in a manner resembling the entry into another's body (*parapurapraveśa*).
For example:

“How can he not partake of bodilessness— he who has destroyed the faculty of discernment, whose mind is perverted, and who feels no compassion for his wife when she is as delicate as a plantain leaf while he strikes her?”
Regarding this point:
"How could this Madana, whose banner bears the sea-monster and who stands upon the foundation of discernment, not be an object of veneration,
since he strikes with arrows born of flowers the bodies of the deer-eyed women that are as graceful as plantain trees?"
A *pratikañcuka* is the depiction of an object that is dissimilar by way of another mode.
For example:
“Bearing a stream of honey falling from the Lord of Honey, which possesses a luster equal to the eyes of an intoxicated *cakora* bird...”
With a heart-pleasing lotus stalk grasped at the tip of her beak, she shone like a female swan holding a cup made of moonstones.
In this regard:
"A certain woman shone while offering wine with a coral-stalked vessel,
as if holding a garland of dried meat with her beak, by means of the cupped hands of her pet parrot."
The transference of objects (*vastusaṃcāra*) consists in the substitution of one object of comparison for another.
For example:
“As if bound with a dense cord of white lotuses, as if bathed by an overflowing stream of milk,”
He was as if entirely swallowed by her wide-expanded eyes, and forcibly drenched as if by a dense cloud of nectar.
Regarding this matter:
“Like ropes of pearls, like garlands of the moon’s digits, like waves from the ocean of milk, like streams of nectar that dispel fatigue—
having suddenly crossed the river of their long side-glances, those eyes of the bee-eyed maidens, graced by the power of their play and instantly radiant with the weight of love, consecrated me.”
The transformation of a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) by means of a semantic ornament (*arthālaṅkāra*) is *dhātuvāda*. For example:
“Victorious are [the feet] caressed by the crest-jewel of the demon Bāṇa, and kissing the circle of the crest-jewels of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.”
The dust from the feet of Tryambaka, which destroys worldly existence, rests upon the crests of the lords of both the gods and the asuras.
Regarding this point:

"Victorious are the dust-particles from the feet of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva), which possess unprecedented activity and have rendered living beings free from passion through their maturity in illuminating the true path."
*Satkāra* (honoring) is the transformation of that very same object by means of excellence.
For example:
"Now, the weight of the hips, having become familiar with the sprouts of the locks of hair—moist from bathing, trembling as the braided tresses are loosened—" [and so forth].
Furthermore, the sporting swans, standing with necks upturned, drink row upon row of water droplets falling from these [clouds] into the sky from the eyes of the lily-eyed women.
In this regard:

"May those drops of water protect you—drops which, falling from the tip of the creeper-like braid of Lakṣmī as she emerged from the Ocean of Milk, were as beautiful as the thread for stringing pearls;

drops that were long gazed upon by Viṣṇu with eyes full of longing for their excellence, and which tasted like nectar as they were playfully licked by the female swans of Varuṇa who had raised their necks."
The living *cīvaka* bird was similar at first, but later became different—
just as [it is said]:
"In the eyes, the belly, the cheeks, and in the ornaments consisting of clusters of radiant jewels..."
With the entire disc of the moon reflected within her, she appeared as if adorned with a hundred moons.
Regarding this point:
"The beautiful woman shines as if attended by the moon, which is reflected in her radiant cheeks, earrings, bracelets, and the clusters of gems on her girdle,
its own form eclipsed by the splendor of her lovely face."
The *bhāvamudrā* is the composition based on the intended meaning of a previous statement;
for example:
“In lands where betel vines entwine the areca-nut trees, and where cardamom creepers embrace the sandalwood trees...”
Be gracious and sport forever on the Malaya plateaus, where the ground is strewn with leaves of the tamāla tree.”
Regarding this point:
"Surely that very Madana presides over even insentient things through the power of yoga,
since the cardamom creeper here embraces the sandalwood tree, and the nāga-creeper climbs the betel-nut tree."
The arrangement of objects that obstructs the intended meaning is its opposite (*tadvirodhinī*).
For example:
“A necklace upon the breast, a jasmine petal bright with ivory leaf-designs upon the ear, a garland upon the head, a slender body clad in fine silk, and breasts white as camphor.”
A drop of sandalwood paste upon your face, a young lotus-stalk white as the moon in your hand—O beautiful one, is this attire of yours white because you have learned it from the autumnal moon?

On this point: "O fawn-eyed one, it is true that during the festival of the lover's tryst, the darkness acted as your stylist for your attire: your form was clad in dark silk; musk served as the decorative leaf-patterns on every limb; your arms bore bracelets of deep-blue gems; a necklace of emeralds graced your neck; and your face was adorned with a creeper-like tress hanging down."
Thus, thirty-two means of seizing the meaning have been demonstrated;
my poetic skill lies therein, in the discernment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.
Furthermore, these means of appropriation should be understood as having their opposites;
the state of being an opposite is to be known through the reversal of the object.

Furthermore—how many who know the science of words and their meanings do not compose poetry? For the entirety of verbal expression is but the eye for one whose wealth is the sacred revelation (*śruti*).
Rather, that which exists as a novel subject matter within speech belongs to those who weave together excellent sayings; his words are pure, standing at the forefront of such authors.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, concerning the varieties such as "the painting-like" (ālekhyaprakhya) in the theft of meaning, within the first section on the secrets of the poet in the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.
Chapter Fourteen:
The Poetic Convention (Kavisamaya). This chapter establishes the conventions regarding genus (jāti), substance (dravya), and action (kriyā).
That meaning which poets compose—though it be unscriptural, non-worldly, and handed down through tradition—is known as *kavisamaya* (poetic convention).
[Objection: "But surely this is a fault;
how then can it be worthy of composition?"
"Thus say the teachers.
"How can this be a fault when it favors the path of poetry? says Yāyāvarīya.
"In that case, the cause must be stated," say the teachers.
"This is what is being stated," says Yāyāvarīya.
For the ancient scholars, having plunged into the Veda with its thousand branches and its auxiliary limbs, and having mastered the treatises, [composed this work].

Having wandered through other lands and other islands, whatever matters they perceived and composed, even though those things may have become otherwise due to the influence of different places and times, the fact that they are recorded as being exactly so is "poetic convention" (*kavisamaya*).
This term *kavisamaya* has become conventionalized through usage by those who see only the application [of the term] without perceiving its original basis.
In that regard, some matter is established as primary according to poetic convention, while some is introduced by rogues for their own purposes under the pretext of another's undertaking;
and that [matter] is threefold: celestial, terrestrial, and subterranean.
Among those pertaining to heaven and the netherworld, that which pertains to the earth is primary,
for it has a vast scope;
and it is fourfold, by virtue of its objects being genus, substance, quality, or action.
Those [types of perception] are also threefold: from the basis of what is non-existent, from the lack of a basis even for what exists, and from necessity.
In that regard, there is a basis for what does not exist as a universal,
such as lotuses, water-lilies, and so forth in rivers,
or swans and the like even in a mere reservoir of water.
And gold, jewels, and so forth, upon those various mountains;
and the lotuses of the rivers, as it is said:
“Prolonging at dawn the sweet, indistinct warbling of the cranes, and fragrant with the intimacy of the scent of blooming lotuses...”
There, the breeze from the Śiprā river, which is so favorable to the limbs of women, removes the fatigue of lovemaking, like a beloved husband who utters flattering words of entreaty.

He beheld the river Jāhnavī, who, with her beauty like a forest of blue water-lilies, was stealing away the drops of sweat from the sky-dwellers— drops acquired through their graceful sport of traveling through the air— with gentle breezes; she was like the daughter of the Sun, who had offered her embrace as a gift.
The same applies to the *nadīkumuda* and other such flowers.
Just as swans [reside] in mere water, it is said:
"There has been, there is, and there will be in this world a person who is blessed, wealthy, and righteous—one who, like Kṣīra Keśava, shall once again establish the glorious Kuḍuṅgeśvara."
With the blended cries of flocks of swans and cranes gently swaying, that new river seems to proclaim with its waters whatever deeds he has performed.
Regarding gold as large as a mountain, as it is said:

"This place, a dwelling for nāgas, delightful with variegated ships, and its surrounding range filled with the abundance of gold, has attained a friendship with the ocean due to their similarity; therefore, it is known as Jīmūtabhartṛ (the Lord of Clouds)."
Regarding jewels, as it is said:
"On the slopes of the mountain, where masses of rays from sapphire gems emit sprays of mist like the hissing breath of great elephants,
the peacocks look on with joy, stretching out their necks like tubes, in the belief that these are clouds."
The same applies to other cases as well;
there is also non-connection despite existence, such as: "There are no mango trees in spring."
There are no flowers or fruits on sandalwood trees, nor fruit on *aśoka* trees.
Regarding these, the first is as follows:
“Caitra, who turns his back on mālatī flowers yet blossoms with an abundance of other blossoms—how is it that those of low birth, though they possess fine minds, are not beloved? This is a wonder.”
The second [verse]:
"Even though the sandalwood tree was fashioned by fate to be devoid of fruit and flowers,
nevertheless, it dispels the distress of others by its very body."
The third [verse]:
"When the fruit depends on fate, what can be done? But in this matter we say: the sprouts of the *aśoka* tree are not equal to the foliage of other trees."
Restriction (*niyama*) is the practice of those whose activities extend over many places, confining them to one;
for example, sea-monsters (*makara*) only in the oceans, and pearls only in the Tāmraparṇī river.
Of these two, the first is:
"The prideful display of the tusks of the sea-monster is worthy of praise as he leads his ancestral domain, marked with his own name and seal, into the ocean while his kinsmen look on."
The second [verse]:
"Granted, let there be rivers on earth with firm foundations, and let their waters be sweet and their shells be fine;
yet, O lady of excellent complexion, apart from this Tāmraparṇī, the wish-granting cow of pearls cannot exist elsewhere."
There is also a basis for [the perception of] a substance even when it does not exist;
for example, the state of being graspable by the fist and the state of being pierceable by a needle in the case of darkness,
and the state of being carried away by a jar in the case of moonlight.
Therein, first:

"It makes the quarters as if slender at their tips, the circle of the earth as if merely the space traversed by a footstep, and the sky as if no larger than the height of an earthenware pot; it makes the darkness graspable by the fist."
And so it is said:
"Even when the prison is shut, in the darkness that can be pierced only by the tip of a needle's point,
and even when my eyes are closed, the face of my beloved remains clearly manifest."
The second [stanza]:
"That moonlight which formerly bore the beauty of a stream from the inner petals of a ketaka flower squeezed by a machine— a luster fit for being woven into a string of pearls—
is now such that it must be poured out with jars, caught in hollowed palms, and drunk with sprouts of lotus stalks, as the splendor of the moon has waned."
It is the lack of a basis for that which exists as a substance;
for example, the moonlight during the dark fortnight,
or the darkness during the bright fortnight.
Of these two, the first is: "There in Yāghatrā, Balabhadra and Hṛṣīkeśa were beheld by the people with curiosity, like white and black wings."
The second [verse]:
"Month after month, the moonlight is equal in both the bright and dark fortnights;
yet of these two, only that which has attained brightness is acquired through deeds of fame."
The restriction of substance is as follows: for example, Malaya alone is the place for sandalwood,
and Himavat alone is the place of origin for birch bark.
Among these, the first is:
"Skilled at removing heat, a dwelling for serpents, and beloved by the gods—
the sandalwood tree is seen nowhere other than on Mount Malaya."
The second [verse]:
"Where birch-bark, inscribed with letters by means of mineral juice and reddened by the spots of elephants,
serves the purpose of love-letters for the beautiful Vidyādhara maidens."
As for the poetic convention regarding miscellaneous matters (*prakīrṇaka-dravya*), it is as follows:
the identity of the milk-ocean and the salt-ocean, and likewise of the *sāgara* and the *mahāsamudra*.
Of these two, the first—
"Let Hari sleep; let there be the infinite jewel within which Lakṣmī is born—of this we have no dispute, O friend!
But alas, for a creature parched with thirst who is far, far away, what is the use of that water in a well? It is the lowest of all."
The second [verse]:
"He saw before him the Gaṅgā, the beloved of the virtuous ocean, who seemed to be threatening the rivers with the knitting of her eyebrows in the form of rolling waves."
There is also the depiction of an action that does not actually exist,
such as the separation of the ruddy goose pair at night to take refuge on different banks, and the drinking of moonlight by the cakora birds.
Among these, the first is:
"By shortening the nights, by diminishing the floods of rivers,
and by [reducing] the lifespan of those called 'wheel-birds' (geese), what has not been done for the benefit of the summer heat?"
The second [verse]:
"O gazelle-eyed one, these are those banks of the rivers near the Malaya mountains, the beloved dwelling-place for the practice of archery of the divine Mind-born (Kāma).
Upon them, during nights dark with the moon, female cakora birds—having drunk in the darkness—drink the pearl-like moonlight with their beaks wide open and their throats quivering."
Even when the purpose for an action exists, there may be no manifestation of it;
for example, the lack of blooming in blue lotuses during the day, and the lack of opening in *śephālikā* flowers at night.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"Having painted a beautiful lotus on the face of Rāma— which was like the orb of the moon momentarily honored by her presence—
a female friend said, 'Now the time for this [lotus] to bloom again has arrived,' and placed a blue water-lily upon her ear."
The second [verse]:
"‘In separation from you, I have been scorched for the entire day by the sun with its fierce rays’—
as if speaking this sorrow to the moon, the śephālikā flower weeps with tears of blossoms."

But there is a restriction (*niyama*), as follows: although the crying of cuckoos is possible at the beginning of summer and so forth, it is restricted (*nibandha*) to spring alone; and the crying and dancing of peacocks are restricted to the rainy season alone.
Of these two, the first—
“In spring, the lotuses submerged within the water rose up as if desiring to hear the song sung in the forest by the cuckoo, who was afraid of the cold.”
The second [verse]:
“Having fanned their tails into circles, the peacocks dance with sweet songs from their throats at the time when the sky is garlanded with clouds.”
This is the convention of poets concerning genus, substance, and action;
following that, it is now described as pertaining to qualities, whether celestial or subterranean.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Establishment of Conventions regarding Genus, Substance, and Action," within the first section, "The Secret of the Poet," of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.
Chapter Fifteen:
The Establishment of the Nature of the Guṇas; the Bondage of the Guṇa of Ignorance (Tamas).
For example: fame, laughter, and the like possess whiteness; infamy, sin, and the like possess blackness; and anger, passion, and the like possess redness.
Regarding the whiteness of his fame:

“Not even a slight stiffness remains in their limbs; their breathing is uninterrupted; their very gaze remains fixed as if submerged in the midst of the ocean of milk—and yet we clearly exist! What manner of thing is this?

Thus, because their expansion is obstructed by the walls of the quarters, the fawn-eyed women marvel at your fleshy glories, which have whitened the three worlds and find it difficult to remain even slightly contained.”
Regarding the whiteness of his laughter: "Under the guise of his loud laughter,
the oceans of milk— white as a mass of foam— seem to pour forth from his mouth as if they had been drunk during the dissolution of the world."
Disrepute is blackness:
"Your glories and the infamies of your enemies spread forth simultaneously,
like garlands of jasmine entwined with blue lotus petals every day."
The blackness of sin:
"The body of the horse-necked one (Haya-kandhara) became darkened by the lines of his sword-blade, which was stainless and drawn forth;
it was as if stained by the impurity of sin produced at that very moment by his resolve to destroy the lineage of Keśava out of sudden wrath."
Regarding his redness with rage: “By the terrestrial [deity], whose body was pale-red from the spreading radiance of his anger reflected upon the surface of the palace floor,
and who filled the belly of the subterranean realm with his intensity, the earth shook as if its interior were trembling.”
An example of being colored by passion (*anurāga-raktatā*) is as follows: “By your fame spreading forth, mingled with affection for your virtues,
half-marks of saffron have suddenly appeared upon the faces of the women who are the quarters of the sky.”
There is also the non-connection of a quality even when it exists,
such as the redness of kunda buds and the teeth of a lover,
or the greenness of lotus buds and the like.
The yellow hue of *priyaṅgu* flowers and the lack of redness in *kunda* buds [are mentioned]—
