“revealed by the smiles from the tips of her *kunda*-bud-like teeth, which illuminate the interior of the assembly.”
His speech became pure in color, as if suddenly cleansed.
The greenness of the lotus bud:

“May the body of Śauri, whose peak reaches the clouds, protect us—his form that displayed the sport of the Primeval Boar, while he raised up the earth submerged in the salt waters of the ocean with his tusk, which touched it as it was mistaken for the bud of a white lotus on a long stalk; and which caused a tumultuous clamor from the hosts of gods and demons agitated at that time.”
The yellowish-green hue of the priyaṅgu flower:
"The ocean produces clear wealth of pearls, as if to adorn the dark priyaṅgu-like breasts of the apsarases."
The restriction of qualities (guṇaniyama), however, is as follows: when the general category is taken up, there is redness in rubies, whiteness in flowers,
and whiteness in clouds.
And the blackness of the clouds.
Regarding that, the first [verse] says:
"Bringing forth [offerings] incessantly by sea-traders, gathered upon the dark lines of thickets on the shore with deceptive means..."
O long-eyed one, do these lotus stalks here cause you to suspect that it is the reflection of the sun rising from within a cloud?

Regarding the whiteness of her smile: "If a flower were set upon a sprout, or if a pearl were placed within a bright coral, then it might resemble that pure smile of hers, whose luster spreads across her dark lips."
Regarding the cloud-blackness:
"With hair as dark as a cloud, the king of celestial chariots, its sacrificial altar purified,
shone like a heap of jewels with a great sapphire in its center."
Of black and blue, of black and green, and of black and dark.
The identification of yellow with red, and of white with pale, is a convention of poets. But how can there be an identity between black and blue?
“Karna also quickly followed the river whose sandy banks were ascended by women from the south; it crossed the Varṇā, which had garlands of cane growing on the trees along both its shores.
Thereafter, the dark mass of its own waters shines high upon the Sahya mountain, like the thick tresses of hair disheveled over the broad shoulder of a beautiful-haired woman.”
The identity of Kṛṣṇa and Hari: "May that water of both the Yamunā, resembling emerald, and the Gaṅgā, as pure as crystal slabs— water which is like the united bodies of Hari and Hara— purify you."
The identity of Kṛṣṇa and Śyāmala:
"O beautiful one, this grove on the slope of Mount Meru rejoices—its trees possessing trunks as smooth as moonstones, its pearl-stones bathed by the Mandākinī;
there, during the dark nights, the celestial wish-fulfilling tree, delighting in the company of unrestrained divine damsels, pours forth moonlight that mingles with the evening breezes."
The identity of yellow and red:
"With a streak shining like pure coral, the moon dispelled the darkness;
with a tusk as orange as a fracture of gold, like the Primeval Boar [lifting] the orb of the earth."
The identity of "white" (śukla) and "pale-white" (gaura):

"Know me to be Kumbhodara, the son of Nikumbha, a servant of the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva), whose back has been purified by the grace of his placing his foot upon it as he desired to mount his bull, pale-white as Mount Kailāsa."
The same applies to other colors as well;
there is a description of the eye and so forth as having multiple colors.
Among those, the whiteness of the eye—
"While I stood in the courtyard of her house in the evening, amidst a crowd of people, my body weary and languid, she— her door gently swaying with her slow steps—
let fall a shower of side-glances moist with love, white as the crescent moon, while she sighed there with a face bowed down by shame."
Darkness—
"Then the protector of the earth, who was like Śarva himself, having spent several nights on the road at the residence of Rama-kṛt-upakārya,
entered Ayodhyā once again, where the windows were turned blue by the eyes of the women gazing at Maithilī."
“O Dark One—

there, the courtesans, their hands weary from waving fly-whisks whose handles jingle against their girdles as they are playfully shaken, and whose handles are encrusted with the luster of gems upon their ribs,
will cast at you side-long glances as long as a row of bees, once they have received from you raindrops as pleasant as nail-marks.”

“Having crossed that [river], proceed, making your own form the object of the curiosity of the women of Daśapura— women whose eyes possess a variegated luster shining above as they lift their lashes, which are accustomed to the play of creeper-like brows, and which steal the beauty of bees following tossed *kunda* flowers.”
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, "The Establishment of the Conventions of the Qualities," in the first section, "The Secret of the Poet," of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.
Chapter 16: The Conventions of Poets (Kavisamaya) 16
Regarding the establishment of poetic conventions (*kavisamaya*) concerning heaven and the netherworld: the poetic convention regarding heaven is similar to that of the earth;
however, the distinction is the identification of the hare and the deer within the moon.
For example:
"Do not fear, O Moon! There is no Rāhu in my wine; Rohiṇī dwells in the sky—why do you tremble, O timid one?"
"Generally, the minds of men waver during encounters with clever women; what is there to wonder at in this?"
And as it is said:
"The moon has a deer placed upon its lap, yet it is marked by a deer;
the lion is the lord of beasts, yet he is pursued by the deer of cruel kings."
The identity of the crocodile and the fish on the banner of Kāma is as follows:
“Take up your bow made of flowers; let the crocodile be raised as your banner; and let your five arrows, which pierce the target of the heart, be once more in your hand.
Some semblance of your form has been burnt away—since you are Kāma, why do you hide? Show your true form! There is no fear here of Śaṅkara; we are all Vaiṣṇavas.”
And as it is said:
"You bear the fish-banner and are not one whose bow is made of flowers; yet, O revealer of dalliance, you possess the nature of the Mind-born (Manmatha).
Nevertheless, O Lord of Men, such lamentations of a beloved woman separated from you have been experienced by me for a long time."
And as it is said:

“Just as the son of the Wind [Hanumān] leaped over the terrifying shore of the great ocean of the Yādavas— which bore the sign of fish turned back in terror by the sound ‘hā’— and lifted up Mount Droṇa, so shall I lift up the Lord of the Ocean who is churned by the wind of my sudden onset.”
The identity of the moon born from the ocean of Atri’s eye:

“Worthy of veneration are the self-born progenitors of the universe, the teachers at the beginning of the ages; among them, Atri fixed the light born of his eyes upon the sky, and that became the moon.
Of that moon, one digit serves as the jewel adorning the crest of Lord Śambhu, while from the remaining digits, those who subsist on *svāhā* and *svadhā* eternally obtain the nectar.”

Even though he has been born for a long time, Śiva’s moon remains ever youthful: “May the crescent of the young moon purify you— the swan of the celestial river appearing as a garland, the flower upon the creeper of Śiva’s matted locks, and possessing the beauty of a mirror for the playful charms of Pārvatī.”
And the embodied nature of desire is as follows:
"This is that Śaṅkara, whose self-restraint is celebrated throughout the three worlds; now, distressed by separation, he bears a womanly form in his body.
'By him we have surely been defeated!'—thus saying, Love triumphs, laughing as he strikes his beloved's hand with his own."
And as it is said:
"The bow is a garland, the bowstring a swarm of humming bees, the target is a woman, and the heart is the mark to be pierced—these are his five arrows, whose first is sound.
May that God of Love, whose power is such that he conquers the three worlds, and who dwells in the side-long glances of his beloved, grant you all your desires."
The unity of even the twelve Ādityas:
“May He protect you—He whose discus, blazing below, above, and all around without end with its horses, performs at great speed the sport of a whirling firebrand for the universe;
and who, with His lofty staff-like rays that rival straight arrows of molten gold, brings the entire mass of intense darkness to its end.”

And as it is said concerning Nārāyaṇa and Mādhava: “May that Mādhava—who, having destroyed the mind-born [Kāma], turned the body of Bali into a woman in former times; who bore the Gaṅgā; who brought about the destruction of Andhaka;
who is fond of peacock feathers; and whose praiseworthy name the immortals call ‘the one who took the moon-adorned head’—protect you, he who wears serpents as his necklace and bracelets.”
In this way, [the names] Dāmodara, Śeṣa, Kūrma, and so forth [are derived].
And as for Kamalā and Saṃpad, it is as follows:
"She who was raised from the ocean by Mandara, which was slowly whirled by his arms; she whom, having himself become a tortoise in ancient times, he supported upon the tip of his hump."
Then that Supreme Person, having made her his target, by means of the gestures of his playfully arched creeper-like eyebrows, established the earth upon the arms of his lovers within their homes.
The poetic convention (kavisamaya) pertaining to the subterranean realm (pātālīya), like those concerning the earth and heaven,
is as follows: therein, there is an identity between the *nāga* and the serpent—
“O King of the *nāgas*, firmly encircle with your coils the broad lower slope of Mount Mandara!”
What excessive burden could there be for you, who have mastered the practice of reclining upon the couch of the playful union with the bull that is difficult to endure?

The unity of the Daityas, Dānavas, and Asuras is as follows: therein, Hiraṇyākṣa, Hiraṇyakaśipu, Prahlāda, Virocana, Bali, Bāṇa, and others are the Daityas; Vipracitti, Śambara, Namuci, Puloman, and so forth are the Dānavas.
The asuras such as Vala, Vṛtra, Vikṣura, Svarbhānu, and Vṛṣaparvan—
regarding their alliance, it is said:
"Victorious are those [feet] caressed by the crest-jewels of the asura Bāṇa, and kissing the circle of the crest-jewel of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa."
The dust from the feet of Tryambaka, which destroys worldly existence, rests upon the crests of the lords of the gods and demons.
And as it is said:

"Who could conquer that fish-bannered god who has conquered the three worlds— he whose arrow is as sharp as the thunderbolt of the demon Śambara, whose staff-like arms are reddened by the rays of the jewels in his armlets, and upon whose broad shoulders rest the decorative leaf-patterns from the breasts of his beloved?"
And as it is said:
"There is a Daitya named Hayagrīva, in whose friendly dwellings those Śrīs—
whose smiles are like white umbrellas— proclaim the strength of his arms."
And as it was said concerning Hayagrīva: "O Lord of the Dānavas, why is this arm of yours not further employed as an ally for Kṛtānta in accomplishing his intentions for universal destruction?"
And as it is said:
"In this great assembly of asuras, there is not even a single asura whose chest has not been polished by the impact of the thunderbolt."
In this way, there are other varieties as well:
"This is the convention of poets, which exists in poetry like a soul;
it has now been explained here by us according to our own understanding."

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Establishment of the Conventions of Poets Belonging to Heaven and the Netherworld," in the first section, "The Secret of the Poet," of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.
Chapter Seventeen:

The Distinction Between Place and Time. Regarding that, the distinction of place: by distinguishing between place and time, the wise man does not lack wealth in the direction of perceiving his purpose.
The world (*jagat*) and its single parts are "places" (*deśa*).
Some say: "The world is one, consisting of heaven and earth. Regarding this, they say:
“Halahala! One ox belongs to Balarāma, yet he has no plow; Viṣṇu possesses land measured by his strides, yet he has neither cow nor plow.
Even today, their agriculture does not flourish without a second cow. Nowhere in this entire world has such a destitute family been seen.”
"Others say that heaven and earth are two worlds. Regarding this, they say:
"His imperishable fame fills both heaven and earth as far as it extends."
For so long, it is said, this virtuous man shall occupy the station of the gods.
"Some say that there are three worlds, distinguished as heaven, the mortal realm, and the netherworld (pātāla). Regarding this, they say:
'O Lord, you alone are the netherworld; you are the binding support of the quarters.'"
And you alone, being the source of the breezes from the chowries, serve as the life-sustainer for the three worlds.
Others say: "Those very [worlds] are *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*.
Regarding this, they say:
"Salutations [to you], as if from the burden of exhaustion caused by supporting the expanse of the three worlds."
"To the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who reclines upon the couch-like body of the Lord of Nagas."
"Others say: 'The True Being is together with these: the great people, austerity, and truth.
Regarding this, they say:
'She who supports the earth with her broad hips [the clouds], and flows along with the moving banner-hands of the water-bearing clouds...'"
This row of palaces with their lofty pinnacles shines forth for Harṣa, whose vast fame is celebrated throughout the six worlds.
"Some say: 'Those [seven] together with the six masses of wind make fourteen.
They say:
'That which remains without limit and without support, following after the manifold elaborations of its own curiosity...'"
"First, may you, the Lord in the form of the Tortoise, who is the root-bulb for the creeper of the fourteen worlds, be victorious here!"
“Some say that these, together with the six Pātālas, are twenty-one.
They say:
“Their splendors are like the laughter of Hara, the abode of Hara, and the necklace of Hara.”
May your glories smear the twenty-one worlds.
“Everything is appropriate,” says Yāyāvarīya:
when one intends to express no distinction, one uses the singular; but when one intends to express a distinction, one uses the plural.
Among those, Bhūrloka is the earth;
therein are seven great continents:
Jambūdvīpa is in the very center, and beyond it is Plakṣa by name, then Śālmala, and beyond that Kuśa.
The Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara [continents] are situated in concentric circles, each one further outward than the last.
“The Salt Ocean, the Ocean of Wine, the Ocean of Sura-liquor, the Ocean of Clarified Butter, the Ocean of Curd-water,
the Ocean of Milk, and the Ocean of Sweet Water— having encircled these seven excellent mountains, they are situated thus.”
"Some say: 'This Lāvaṇa ocean is but one. Regarding this, they say:

'Herein are eighteen islands, and the earth is extended by nine divisions of its own limbs; there is but one ocean whose waters spread to the ends of the quarters—this is a vast and excellent kingdom.'"
He who grew angry with the Creator, thinking, "He will not give me a share of this heroic valor acquired in some battle or other," [is Śiva].
Others say there are three; they say:
"By him, whose great shaking of the mountains completely and effortlessly overcame the triple ocean..."
By that energy which shattered the compact masses, the wind released at the time of the end of the eon was surpassed.
Or as it is said:

“In the absence of the Mātangas, when the elephants of the quarters—whose faces were once stained with rut—had been driven away and the theft of their pleasure had occurred, wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*) shone forth in every direction.

When the trees of the garden ponds of his enemies had been cut down, he fashioned *kalpavṛkṣa* trees for them; thus, for those who enjoy the fruit of the encircling ocean-tide, there was the mental accomplishment (*mānasī siddhi*).”
Others say there are four. They say:
"Adorned with the beauty of a single-string necklace formed by the waves of the tides of the four oceans..."
"His fame has gone somewhere, having even leaped over Mount Meru."
"Everything is consistent because their underlying intentions differ," says Yāyāvarīya.
However, those who propound the *satpadasamudra* (the ocean of the six categories) do not deviate from the treatise at all;
as they say:
“In the ocean water that remained as the residue of Agastya’s single mouthful,
even Keśava, while crossing it for a mere moment, was treated like a small aquatic insect.”
In the center of Jambudvīpa stands the first of mountains, Meru by name, the king of mountains made of gold;
he is the treasury of embodied medicinal herbs and the abode of all the gods.
“Nevertheless, taking him as the limit, the lotus-born Lord fashioned the creation of the universe— horizontally, upwards, and downwards.”
That Blessed One is Meru, the primary mountain range that encircles the continents. To its four directions lies the region of Ilāvṛta. To the north of it are three mountain ranges of regions.
Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavat; and Ramyaka, Hiraṇmaya,
and the Northern Kurus— these are their three regions (varṣas) in order.
To the south as well, there are exactly three: Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat; [and the regions of] Harivarṣa and Kimpuruṣa.
There are three regions known as Bhārata;
among them, this is the region of Bhārata, which has nine divisions: Indradvīpa, [Kusadvīpa, Tāmradvīpa, Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, Saumyadvīpa, Gāndharvadvīpa, Varuṇadvīpa, and] Ayaḥśṛṅga.
Kaserumān, Tāmraparṇa, and Gabhastimān.
Nāgadvīpa,
Saumya,
and Gandharva.
Varuṇa, and this ninth is Kumārīdvīpa;
there are five hundred [yojanas] of water.

These five regions, distinguished as "the plains" (*sthala*), each extend for a limit of one thousand *yojanas* from the southern ocean to the Himalaya, the king of mountains; they are mutually inaccessible to one another.
He who conquers these is called a sovereign (*sabhṛāj*).
From the city of Kumārīpura to Bindusaras, a distance of one thousand *yojanas*, constitutes the field of the universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
Conquering that [treasure], he becomes a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
As for the marks of a wheel-turning monarch, they are:
"The wheel, the chariot, the jewel, the wife, the treasure, the horse, and likewise the elephant."
"These six jewels have been proclaimed for all universal monarchs."
And here, on the island of Kumārī:
“The Vindhya, the Pāriyātra, the Śuktimat, the Ṛkṣa mountain,
Mahendra, Sahya, and Malaya— these seven are the principal mountain ranges.”
Among those, the Vindhya and others have well-known forms, while there are four specific types of Malaya mountains.
Of these, the first is—

“That land is the birthplace of sandalwood trees that delight all beings, which are entwined by serpents from their very roots and trunks, and of young *jātī* jasmine trees combined with *kakkola*, cardamom, and black pepper.”

The second verse: "That Malaya mountain, whose slopes the wish-fulfilling cow of pearls (Mauktikakāmadhenu) and the Tāmraparṇī river revere, and which is purified by Ratneśvara, the lord of jewels, and by Agastya, the pitcher-born sage, who is a great treasury of gems."
There, the trees are named coral; there, pearls are born within the bamboo stalks;
and in that place, the *dhanasāra* trees burst open at the roars of lions intoxicated with passion.
The third [stanza]:
"The playground of all the gods, the abode of men, and the station of the bull among sages—
there stands that Malaya mountain, a source of wonder with its ever-fruiting flowers, creepers, sprouts, and roots."

The fourth [verse]: "There, that city known as Laṅkā— the royal capital of Rāvaṇa— is adorned with rows of palaces, balconies, and gables variegated with gold and jewels, and its gates bear the marks of the Lord of the Gods fastened by bolts."
"The southern wind, the friend of spring, which causes the cuckoo's song, produces flowers, and grants the birth of the fifth note— blows from the north toward those four as well."
Āryāvarta is the region between the eastern and western oceans and the Himavat and Vindhya mountains;
therein exist the four castes and the four stages of life,
which are the root of virtuous conduct.
The local usage there generally belongs to poets. In that regard, the eastern region lies to the east of Vārāṇasī, where [there are] Aṅga, Kaliṅga, Kosala, and Tośala (or Toṣa).
The regions include Loṭaka, Magadha, Mudgara, Videha, Nepāla, Puṇḍra, Prāgjyotiṣa, Tāmalipta, Kāmala, Daṇḍa, Malla, Vartaka, Suhyas, Brahmottara, and others.
The mountains include Bṛhadgṛha, Lohitagiri, Cakora, Dardura, Nepāla, Kāmara, and so forth.
The rivers are the Śoṇa and the Lauhitya.
There are rivers such as the Gaṅgā, Karatoyā, and Kapiśā;
there is the production of lavalī, granthiparṇaka, aguru, drākṣā, kastūrikā, and so forth;
and beyond Māhiṣmatī lies the Deccan (Dakṣiṇāpatha).

Therein lie the provinces of Mahārāṣṭra, Māhiṣaka, Āśmaka, Vidarbha, Kuntala, Kratha, Kaiśika, Sūrpāraka, Kāñcī, Kerala, Kāvera, Murala, Vānavāsaka, Siṃhala, Coḍa, Daṇḍaka, Pāṇḍya, Pallava, Gāṅga, Nāśikya, Kauṅkaṇa, Kollagiri, Vallara, and others;
as well as the mountains such as the southern foot of the Vindhya range, Mahendra, Malaya, Mekala, Pālamañjara, Sahya, Śrīparvata, and so forth.
The rivers beginning with the Narmadā, Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Godāvarī, Kāverī, Bhaimarathī, Veṇā, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Vañjurā, Tuṅgabhadrā, Tāmraparṇī, Utpalāvatī, Rāvaṇagaṅgā, and others [flow here].
Their origin has been explained by the account of the origin of the Malaya mountains.
Beyond the Devasabhā mountain lies the western region.
Therein are the districts (janapadas) such as Devasabha, Surāṣṭra, Daśeraka, Travaṇa, Bhṛgukaccha, Kacchīya, Ānarta, Arbuda, Brabrahmaṇavāha, and Yavana;
the mountains (parvatas) such as Govardhana, Giri, Nagara, Devasabha, Mālyaśikhara, Arbuda, and others;
and the rivers (nadyaḥ) such as the Sarasvatī, Śvabhravatī, Vārtaghnī, Mahāhiḍimbā, and so forth.
There is the production of *karīra*, *pīlu*, *guggulu*, dates, wild asses, and so forth.
Beyond Pṛthūdaka lies the Northern Region (*Uttarāpatha*),

where dwell the Śakas, Kekayas, Vokkāṇas, Hūṇas, Vāṇāyujas, Kāmbojas, Vālīkas, Valavas, Limpākas, Kulūtas, Kīras, Taṅgaṇas, Tuṣāras, Turuṣkas, Barbaras, Harahas, Urahvas, Hūhakas, Sahuḍas, Haṃsamārgaras, Ramaṭhas, Karakaṇṭhas, and others.
The provinces;
the mountains such as the Himālaya, Kalinda, Indrakīla, and Candrācala;
and the rivers such as the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Sarasvatī, Śatadrū, Candrabhāgā, Yamunā, Airāvatī, Vitastā, Vipāśā, Kuhū, and Ikṣu.
The production of *sarala* pine, *devadāru* cedar, *drākṣā* grapes, saffron, fine skins, *sauvīra*, *srotoñjana*, rock salt, *saindhava* salt, lapis lazuli, and horses occurs there;
among these, the term "Middle Country" (*madhyadeśa*) is used by poets.
Furthermore, he is not one who fails to follow the meaning of the treatises.
Regarding this, they say:
"The region between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa."
In this regard, those regions, mountains, rivers, and the production of commodities that are well-known through established convention have not been specifically described.
As for the regions, mountains, and rivers of other continents,
they are not very useful to poets and thus have not been deeply considered.
“The region between Vinaśana and Prayāga, and between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers, is Antarvedī;
one should divide the directions with reference to that,” so say the Teachers.
“Even there, one should take Mahodaya as the central point,” says the descendant of Yāyāvara.
Some maintain that "the division of directions is indeterminate because the directions themselves are not fixed.
For instance, what is to the east of Vāmanasvāmin is to the west of Brahmaśilā;
and what is to the south of Gādhipura is to the north of Kālapriya.
"Form is that which is bound by limits, whereas the other [qualities] are indeed unrestricted," says Yāyāvarīya.
"The four directions are East, South, West, and North," say some. Regarding this, they say:
“In battle, against his enemies in all four directions, he performed with his wondrous deeds a deed unprecedented, without need for a fee, without a successor, and unsurpassed.”
“Aindri, āgneyī,
yāmyā,
nairṛtī,
Some say that the eight directions are Vāruṇī, Vāyavyā, Kauberī, Aiśānī, and [the others].
Regarding this, they say:

“One light [the sun], two in the eyes, three in the world, four declared by the lotus-born [Brahmā], five of beings, and likewise six various kinds in the seasons—those rays of yours, praised by the true lords, gods, and sages, which occupy the eight directions, attain a state of nine at the forenoon of the sun; may those hundreds of rays bestow auspiciousness.”
"Two are Brāhmī and Nāgīyā; together with those, these are ten," say others. They further state:
"Upon a ground made narrow by the boundaries reaching to the very limits of the ten directions..."
"The condition of one who is generous-minded within this village of the universe is precarious."
Let it be so;
for the extent of the directions is dependent upon one's intention to speak. In this regard, within a painting, there is an "east."
In accordance with that is the west; by the pole star is the north; and in accordance with that is the south.
In the intermediate directions are the Vidiśas; above is Brāhmī, and below is Nāgīyā.

The poetic discourse (*vyavahāra*) of poets is of two kinds: that which is established from antiquity (*prāksiddha*), and that which is to be accomplished by means of a specific location as its basis (*viśiṣṭasthānāvadhisādhya*). Regarding the former, the ancients [have said]: “By two or three stars situated in the sky like ancient pearls polished by the touchstone, the female *cakra* birds, languid from their heavy drinking of moonlight, gaze upward.”
The moon, possessing the hue of a parasol of honeyed foam, has departed to the peak of the western mountain, and the eastern quarter has become a vessel for the luster of the eyes of young cats.
“Dakṣiṇa—
desiring to go toward the southern direction, he shone intensely,
like the divine sun desiring to abandon the southern quarter.”
“Look, O you of measured speech! The sun, hanging at the edge of the western quarter,
has fashioned from the waters of the lake a long bridge, as if made of refined gold.”
Uttara said: "In the northern direction there is a deity-essence, the king of mountains named Himālaya;
plunging into the eastern and western oceans, he stands like a measuring rod for the earth."
Regarding the division of directions within a specific spatial limit, the east and west are as follows:
“O aquatic creatures, move together according to your own kind, whether to the east or to the west of Mount Candana;
otherwise, this separation of yours shall not cease until the end of the kalpa, for you are joined by the continuous bridge of mountains.”
Regarding "southern" and "northern," for example:
"In the southern region from the city of Kāñcī, and likewise in the northern direction from the ocean,
the Bodiless One dwells happily with Rati, having made his beautiful bow into a circle reaching to his ears."
In the case of "uttara" and so forth, there is the designation of the northern direction; likewise, in the case of "anuttara" and so forth, there is also the designation of the northern direction.
Of these two, the first—
“There our home stands, visible from afar by its archway as beautiful as Indra’s bow, surpassing the mansions of the Lord of Wealth;
in whose garden grows a young *mandāra* tree, bent with clusters of blossoms, nurtured by my beloved like a fostered son, and within reach of my hand.”
The second [verse]:
"On the northern side of the Sahya mountain, where the Godāvarī river flows—
that region is the most delightful in this entire world."
The same applies to the other directions as well.
In that regard, one should describe the sequence of countries, mountains, rivers, and so forth, as well as the directions, exactly as they are;
however, what is common to both should be established according to worldly convention.
Regarding the rule for their colors:
among them, those from the east are dark-complexioned,
while those from the south are black.
Among those from the west, they are pale; among those from the north, fair; and among those from the Middle Country, they are black, swarthy, and fair.
The "darkness of the eastern quarter":
"Amidst the dark limbs of the women, which steal away all other necklaces with their single strings of pearls,
the bodiless god of love gracefully leaps about, having made his flowery bow into a circle."
The Southern Blackness:
“This orb of the Lord of Rays, resembling a molten golden sphere, is gradually losing its light as its circular disc sinks from the sky;
meanwhile, this mass of darkness, dark as the cheek of a flute-player, spreads toward the east, appearing as if clustered into bouquets by the circles of shadows cast by the trees.”
“The Bakula bud,
with its branches smiling [in bloom], attains the state of a lock of hair for the female bees whose eyes are restless in the sport of devouring honey;
moreover, the luster from the pale cheeks of Western (Yavana) young women now sets foot, though but slightly, upon the leaves of the betel vine.”
“Now the golden *kañcanāra* trees are embraced limb by limb with flowers as fair as the women of the North; the *aśoka* is honored with leaves redder than the wounds from the teeth of *vānīrī* women;
even the *campaka* has become capable of stealing the beauty of the Northern damsels; and with its madder-red buds, the *pāṭala* tree bears a truly unique script.”
Or as it is said:
"The sixteen-carat gold, as if melted, has been set upon the lines of the Kashmiri women's limbs, where the waves of beauty are shimmering."

An example of blackness characteristic of the Middle Country (madhyadeśya) is as follows: "All [the Kauravas] beheld Pāñcālī, who was like a jet-black plume of smoke from the fire of Yudhiṣṭhira’s wrath, which was to utterly consume the Kuru lineage."
Therefore, there is a dark complexion characteristic of the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa).

Furthermore, we have stated in the conventions of poets that on the path of poetry there is no great distinction between dark and black, or between pale and fair; thus, there is also a fair complexion characteristic of the Middle Country.
“Upon your forehead, which is as fair as a lump of fresh butter, the orb of the moon is reflected in the daughter of the Lord of North Kosala,
appearing as if marked by a spot resembling a musk-paste leaf.”
However, the distinction is that in the eastern region, the complexion of princesses and others is fair or pale;
the same applies to the southern region as well.
Among these, the first—

“Gazing repeatedly at Jānakī’s lotus-face— whose cheeks steal the luster of an elephant calf’s tusks and whose blossoming thrills of love manifest as a spreading horripilation— and hearing the tumultuous clamor of the night-stalking army, the Lord of the Raghus tightens the knot of his matted locks.”
The second [verse]:
"Among all those wives of Mādhava, who possessed the luster of the moon,
Rukmiṇī blazed forth like the science of grammar among all branches of knowledge."
In this way, other [faults] as well should be inferred according to their possibility:
scholars declare that what is contrary to the stated method is "contrary to place" (deśaviruddha).
That must be avoided with effort; however, the examples cited therein are for the sake of illustrating the faults.
Thus has the division of the regions been briefly outlined by me for the sake of the wise; but he who desires to know more should consult my *Bhuvanakośa*.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, "The Classification of Regions," in the first section, "The Secret of the Poet," of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara.
Chapter 18:
The Division of Time. Time is distinguished by its divisions, such as *kāṣṭhā* and the rest.
Fifteen *nimeṣas* are said to be one *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty *kāṣṭhās* are called a *kalā*.
Thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*, and thirty *muhūrtas* make up a day and night combined.
These two occur during the months of Caitra and Āśvayuja.
Following Caitra, for three months there is a daily increase of the day and a decrease of the night by one muhūrta each month;
after that, there is a daily increase of the night and a decrease of the day by one muhūrta each month.
After the full moon of Āśvayuja, this very process is reversed:
the month of the sun's passage from one zodiac sign to another is the [solar] month; beginning with the rainy season, it is the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana).
The period beginning with the winter solstice is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa); a year consists of two such courses—this is the solar measurement.
A fortnight (pakṣa) consists of fifteen days and nights.
The month of the ancestors (pitrya) is measured by the moon: it is bright when the moon is waxing and dark when its blackness is increasing;
and by this [measure], the entire ritual procedure ordained in the Vedas is established.
The lunar month is that which has its fortnights reversed from the ancestral (pitrya) order;
this is the standard adopted by the inhabitants of Āryāvarta and by poets.
And thus, two fortnights constitute a month.
Two months constitute a season (ṛtu).
Six seasons make a year (saṃvatsara). And that [year] begins with Caitra, according to the astrologers.
Those who know the ways of worldly life [reckon] by beginning with Śrāvaṇa;
therein, Nabha and Nabhasya are the rainy season (varṣā),
and Īṣa and Ūrja are the autumn (śarat).
Saha and Sahasya are the winter season; Tapas and Tapasya are the cool season;
Madhu and Mādhava are the spring season.
Śukra and Śuci constitute the summer season.
Regarding that, the poets say: "In the rainy season, the wind is from the east.
The teachers say: "It is from the west; the eastern wind, however, is a repeller."
Regarding this, they say: "The rainy season is struck down by the east wind; the autumn is struck down by the west wind.
Regarding this, they say:
“In the rainy season, the sky is completely filled with clouds heavy with water;
winds from the western quarter blow, carrying the fragrance of kadamba flowers.”
“The reality of things is not the governing factor;
the convention of poets is the authority,” says Yāyāvarīya.
Regarding this, they say:

May the Son of Vinatā, the delighter of the Sun, bestow happiness upon you as he approaches his chariot— like the east wind blowing toward the cloud-laden ocean, like smoke rising from a fire, like the primordial creation of the universe, like the sacred *praṇava* which is the supreme purifier of the mass of Vedas, and like the joyful introductory music at the festival of the twilight dance of the Enemy of Madana.
In autumn, the wind blows from no fixed direction, as it is said:
“At dawn, winds blew that carried away the black dewdrops and were fragrant with the astringent scent of the buds within the swelling *śophālī* flowers.”
"In winter, the wind is from the west," say some;
"from the north," say others;
"both [are possible]," says Yāyāvarīya.
Of these two, the western wind is described thus:

“Breaking the rows of trees with their vigorous strength, its bark made rough by the slopes of the Snowy Mountains; shaking the *lañcātaka* birds who are agitated by the mass of thick waves in the roaring waters;

blowing with speed from the west, raining down a shower of fine spray from the fragments of swift-moving ice-stones; and carrying the sound of the *sārasa* cranes as they glide swiftly through the thick resinous sap exuding from trees crushed by elephants—such is the western wind.”
The Northerner says:
“Scattering the curls of women who have bathed, causing their hair-bands to sway, kissing the waters of the Candrabhāgā river with the singular vigor of birch-tree trunks—
these northerly winds blow, fragrant from their intimacy with musk-deer, the beloveds of the Bāhlava women, and the makers of sport for the Kaulūtīs, having familiarized themselves with the snow.”
In the *śiśira* season as well, [the wind] blows from the north or the west, just as in *hemanta*;
in *vasanta*, it blows from the south.
As it has been said:

“Shaking the groves of the forests of Laṅkā, repeatedly causing the creeper-like tresses of the Kerala women to dance, suddenly loosening the braided hair-knots of the Andhra women, and swaying the betel vines—
the southern breeze, fragrant with crushed sandalwood, the companion of the fish-bannered god of love, the friend of the spring season, and the thief of the hearts of women, has arrived.”
“Either the wind from both directions [blows] in summer,” say some; “the Nairṛta wind,” say others;
“both [blow],” says Yāyāvarīya.
Among these, the first [verse] is:
“Thick columns of dust, kissing the surface of the sky with whirlwinds of wind, weave a conjecture of pillars for a future canopy of clouds across the firmament;
moreover, by means of the showers of water from mirages, they thread together the vessels of rivers whose waters have vanished, portending prosperity in days to come.”
The second [verse]:
"This very sun now scorches with rays as if made of fire; the entire earth is covered by a vast expanse of spreading embers;
the wind rains down like hot ashes, and the demon Nairṛta, as well as Madana, strikes with arrows as if made of fire."
Moreover:
"Depositing embryos in the cranes, producing bamboo shoots by their own sounds,
and sealing the dust during the rainy season, the clouds steal away the kings' preparations for military expeditions."
Bestowing blossoms upon the sallakī, sāla, śilīndhra, and yūthī trees, with its lāṅgalī plants in full bloom,
and fragrant with the lovely scent of burnt field-furrows, this season of the clouds is worthy of honor.
The forests are as dark as indigo leaves; the mountains gleam, washed by torrents of rain;
the rivers have their banks breached by the floodwaters; and the grassy meadows are thick with indragopa insects.
This season, which delights the cakora birds, which steals the conduct of ascetics, and along whose path the lords are watched by women separated from their lovers,
has filled the sky with clouds as caravans of travelers set out toward their homes.
That pleasure-trip with amorous women, that bed of playful luxury upon the tops of lofty palaces,
and that sandalwood paste from the heart of musk-deer— [all these have vanished].
She was the first guest-offering for the Lord of the Waters.

The arrival of the clouds releases its poison—the poison of Love—among those separated from their lovers: a poison in which the cātaka birds are restless and fickle; in which the passion of the deer is aroused; in which the frogs strive with loud croaking; in which the serpents are bold with the weight of rut; and in which the cranes and water-fowls rejoice at the dancing of the peacock flocks.

Alas, the end of the summer season captivates the heart: the *kuṭaja* buds are bursting forth in Dalhaṇa; heaps of *nīpa* flowers have blossomed; the *arjuna* trees are laden with clusters of blossoms, kin to the new shoots of the *dhava*;
the sky is turbid with *kadamba* pollen; the *ketakī* buds have been gathered; and the thickets of *nicula* trees are swaying.
The rains.

Autumn approaches, suddenly causing the peacocks to lose their pride while emboldening the ospreys and the bees; it causes the day-lotuses to bloom and brings the night-lotuses and water-lilies to full flower.
She shines as she arranges flowers upon the bandhūka, bāṇāsana, and saffron;
and upon the śephālikā, satpala, palāśa, kāśa, maṇḍīra, saugandhika, and mālatī.
Whose mind does that river not captivate— she who is accompanied by *khañjarīṭa* birds, whose clarity is like the grace of milk,
and who is followed by flocks of *kādaṃba*, *kāraṇḍava*, *cakravāka*, *sārasa*, and *krauñca* birds?
Leading her flock of swans, purifying the waters with the gaze of Agastya,
and bearing within herself a bright embryo of pearls, the autumn shines forth with her wondrous deeds.
Bulls digging the earth with the tips of their hooves, elephants goring the embankments with their tusks,
and ruru deer casting off their worn antlers, make the worlds eager for a new vision.

Here, the sky on all sides has the brilliance of pure white, the luster of moonlight, water, and sapphire; the path of the gods, the descent of the celestial river, and fragments of withered clouds appear pale white.
On the Mahānavamī day, kings intent upon the expedition should perform the worship of all weapons, the lustration ceremony (*nīrājanā*) for their horses, soldiers, and elephants,
and various festivities during the Dīpālikā festival.
In the sky, there is a multitude of stars of increasing brilliance; the earth is fit for the movement of chariots;
the sun possesses radiant rays in autumn; and Mādhava awakens together with the gods.

In the very fields, the *kalamā* rice stalks are bending under the weight of ripening grain; the ancient *āmalaka* fruits turn blue as they ripen; the *ervāruka* cucumbers emit the fragrance of their bursting seeds; and the fruits of the overripe *trapusī* melons are turning sour.
In the courtyards of the farmers' houses, made beautiful by the experience of the fragrance from scattering grains of fresh rice,
the young wives bring joy with the tinkling of their bracelets as their hands move to strike the pestles and shake out the grain.
The sun burns fiercely like a low-born man newly wealthy; the ruru deer sheds its antler like an ungrateful friend;
the water becomes clear like a sage’s reflection on the Dharma; and the mud dries up like a poor man consumed by passion.
In this river, the streams flow with crooked courses, their sandy beds marked by rows of shells and containing tortoises emerging from within;
there, herons extend their formidable beaks in pursuit of fish fleeing through the shallow, rippling water.

"In autumn, the abundant mass of river water recedes— its banks and hollows no longer muddy, its surface brightened by the frantic leaps of carp, its young fish wandering in terror at the cry of falling ospreys, its sands strewn with tumbling tortoises, and made noisy by the clamor of darting herons."
Autumn.

Victorious is the fresh onset of the winter season, in which the mucukunda trees bear two or three buds, the lavalī vines gradually show three or four flower-buds, and the phalinī plants possess five or six blossoms.
Adorned with ear-ornaments of *punnāga* and *rodhra* blossoms, their brows arched and their limbs curved by bodices, these fair-browed women bear their braided tresses—
scented with fragrant oils and marked with wax mixed with saffron shimmering upon their lips.
Just as the winter season flowers forth, its winds scattering heaps of powdered frost,
even so do the breasts of women endowed with youth attain a state of slight warmth here.
Having eaten choice boars, fresh rice-porridge, curds, quivers of arrows,
and very tender mustard shoots, people here disparage the science of medicine.
Here, the customary practice is that food and drink are palatable only when tepid with water;
here one lies down after having crushed an unfortunate woman—may there always be well-being for this winter season!
The peacocks have shed their plumage and are free from intoxication; the boundaries of the fields are overgrown with wheat and barley;
tigresses give birth; and the water is filled with mist—these are the triumphant signs of winter.
In this place, fields ripen with śamī plants and grain;
the nights are marked by three stars, and salts are cooked.

In the winter season, the male cuckoos in the gardens become mute, a seal of silence is placed upon the mouths of female bees, the flight of birds through the sky becomes sluggish, and the pride of serpents is extinguished.
The abundance of ripeness in jujubes and oranges manifests as sugarcane;
within the cores of black sugarcane and pineapples, a certain unprecedented splendor of sweetness is born.

Those for whom there is a palace in their midst, a wealth of couches, and by their side wives whose eyes are like stars in the full bloom of youth—for them, the fire of amorous play has its fierce smoke concealed; they perceive winter as a mere remnant of summer.
Thus ends the description of Hemanta (winter).
Śiśira (the cool season) possesses the same characteristics as Hemanta, with this distinction:
"The night, possessing a length of three watches suitable for amorous dalliance, passes; and the wind blows fiercely, capable of being soothed only by saffron paste."
What else could be more precious here than beds where the cotton mattresses are doubled over, filled with the spreading smoke of aloe-wood incense,
and where young men, having embraced their lovers and drunk in the cold with the exhaustion of extensive lovemaking,
sleep through the long night of thick joy, their feet tucked together and swaying at the joints as they repeatedly turn upon their thighs?

In drinking, there is no distinction between water and wine, whether they are delicious or tasteless; nor is there any difference here between snow and fire in their tactile effects; nor is there any difference in embracing between the unfortunate woman and the beautiful one, nor in serving between the moon and the sun.
The *marubaka* flower is now the object of floral rites; the sport of water is held in contempt; the *kunda* flowers stand at the head of all blossoms;
the orb of the sun enjoys the favor of the moon-marked deer; and sandalwood pastes burn during this frosty season.
Upon the stalks of the *siddhārtha* plants— which, as they progress upward, consist of a succession of dense thorns with increasingly diminished internodes—
where only two or three flowers remain, the process of ripening, following the sequence of their production, imparts a tawny hue.

Now, in the pleasure-pools at the bottom of the water, where the fish lie hidden and the lotus-stalks remain as the only remnants of the plants, struck by the fierce winds from the north, the eye finds no delight.
Intoxicating the elephants, delighting the spotted deer, a boar to the flowers, and a lion to the steadfast;
censured by the poor and praised alone by the wealthy—such is this formidable winter season.
The fire of dried cow-dung is as sweet as the anger of a bride who has not yet been seen; the frosty wind is as cruel as the embrace of a deceitful man;
the radiance of the sun is now dull like that of one whose wealth has vanished; and the moon bears the likeness of the face of a woman separated from her lover.
"Women, by nature prone to heat, with their hips, breasts, arms, thighs, feet, and other parts smeared with heated saffron paste,
utterly dispel even the feverish distress of the cold season for those in the prime of youth who embrace them throughout the entire night."
The cool season.

“In Caitra, the time for intoxication belongs specifically to parrots and starlings, to green pigeons, gallinules, and bees, and to male cuckoos whose kinsman is the mango tree; it is the season of passion in the cities.”
And here, the minds of beautiful women were especially intent upon the graceful dance of amorous play, upon swings and hammocks,
upon song adorned with the exploits of Gaurī, and upon the elaborate worship of the God of Love.
The male cuckoo warbles in the fifth note; the charms of young women manifest with force;
and here in spring, Love fashions his bow-staff anew with fresh blossoms.

In the springtime, when their beloveds have been turned into lovers of memory, the special attire of devoted young women— who wear safflower-dyed garments and vermilion upon their parting lines— becomes truly delicious to the taste.
This is the season when the *karṇikāra* trees stand tall with blossoms, when the *kāñcanāra* is honored by five flowers,
when the *kovidāra* is skilled in its full blooming, and when the *sinduvāra* is ready to open its petals.

In spring, the *rohitaka*, *āmrātaka*, *kiṅkirāta*, *madhūka*, and *moca* trees, along with the *mādhavī* creepers and the *śobhāñjana* tree together with the *kesara*, triumph with their abundance of flowers.
That which is the binding of the hair in the glances of the *mādhavī* buds, that which is the gain in the description of the sweet warbling of the cuckoo,
and that which is the worship of Smara with *damanaka* flowers— this Spring is the venerable teacher of women.

In the month of Caitra, the *kurabaka* has not been embraced, the *talaka* has not been seen, nor has the *aśoka* been kicked by the feet of beautiful-eyed women; the *bakula* has not been sprinkled with mouthfuls of wine—and yet, strangely, they all stand strewn with blossoms.
In the month of Caitra, there are two variegated Aśoka trees, red and blue, and the third is the golden Aśoka, which is yellow;
among all other flowers, its blossoms are victorious over the mind even across the three worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar.
Spring is the cause for arranging flower-garlands from *gūvāka* fruits, coconut trees, *hintāla* palms, *pāṭala*, *sīkiṃśika*, date palms, and young *tāḍa* and *tāḍī* trees.
This summer season brings blossoms to the *mallikā* jasmine,
is delightful with the flowers of the *śirīṣa*, bestows blooms upon the golden *ketakī*, and causes the *dhātakī* trees to flourish.
Having dispelled their languor born of fatigue by means of dates, rose-apples, jackfruit, mangoes, *moca*, *priyāla*, betel nuts, and coconuts, couples here take pleasure in the pursuit of love.
The streams, though waterless, along with the wells and water-stations crowded with travelers on the scorching day,
and the roads, when requested for a drink of barley-meal in the heat, carry forth [the water] both at dawn and at evening.
That which consists of half-day sleep during the daytime, bathing play at the close of day,
and the onset of lovemaking during the remainder of the night— that is the "fist-yoga" (muṣṭiyoga) which destroys the intense heat of summer.
The moonlight, as refreshing as sandalwood paste; the series of ripples from the breeze through the lattice windows;
and the rain of water droplets from palm-leaf fans—these offer a handful of water to the Pure One.
Camphor powder, mango sprigs, betel leaf prepared with fresh areca nuts, pearl necklaces, and fine silken garments— these are the great secret for the practice of cooling.

With pearl necklaces smeared with sandalwood paste, entwined with lotus-fiber garlands and moistened by water, and with wreaths of smiling campaka flowers upon his head— this very man brings the onset of winter even in the summer heat.
For here—“The elements seem to be cooked; the dust-seeds seem to be scorched;
the waters seem to be boiled; and the mountains seem to be melted.”

The black antelopes are lured onto the dry land by mirages; the flow of water has been reduced to mere trickles bound together like reeds; the ponds have their fish gasping for breath due to the scarcity of water; and the wells possess only the circles of buckets that creak as they are drawn up.
Young elephants, śarabhas, and wild asses approach in rut and undergo a transformation;
having ascended the dry lands covered with karavīra and karīra flowers, they remain there.
In the heat of summer, mango juice, *rasālā*, rice with broth, fruit drinks,
milk-shakes, the essence of musk, and boiled milk serve as a medicine that revives the god of love.

With their youth reddened by the application of water and sandalwood paste, their bodies moist with water, and wearing garlands of pearls along with lotuses, they lie upon beds fashioned from plantain leaves; having summoned the God of Love, they seat him at their side.
In summer, the forest edges resound with the chirping of crickets; the bulls, along with their herds of elephants and boars, are smeared with mud;
and the flocks of peacocks and deer have their shoulder-feathers drooping as they shed their plumage.
A delightful mansion with its roof washed by moonlight, wine mixed with water left over from one’s beloved,
and garlands of pale-red jasmine upon the neck— alas, these instantly turn the summer into winter!
Summer.
And the season should be determined according to its four stages, namely:
the transition, infancy, and so forth.
Maturity and non-return;
the junction is the interval between two seasons.
An example of the junction between winter and spring:
“The *kunda* flowers have shed their blossoms; the trees are sluggish in putting forth new flowers; these cuckoos hold their songs within their minds but do not yet utter them.
And yet, the rays of the sun cut through the lingering chill, though they have not yet assumed that harshness which brings on exhaustion.”
The Childhood of Spring: “Flowers are within the buds of the creepers; shoots are in the midst of the sprouts; the fifth note is held merely as a desire within the throats of the female cuckoos.
Moreover, in just two days, the God of Love, victorious over the three worlds, will surely find his long-practiced bow ready for use.”
The Fullness of Spring:
“Now the *vicakila* jasmine attains equality with six-month-old pearls; the *kāñcanāra* flower draws away the splendor from a cloth washed in madder;
the *madhūka* bud acts as a plunderer of the beauty of the Hūṇa women; and the *kesara* flower, resembling the navel of a Lāṭī woman, shines forth as it falls from the tip of its stalk.”

When a characteristic of a season has passed, yet flowers and other signs continue to appear, they call that the "persistence of characteristics" (liṅgānuvṛtti); this is to be understood from the world of poetry.

In the rains, the signs of summer persist in the continued blooming of the lotuses; the sky wears a blanket of clouds as dark as the throat of a *kalaviṅka* bird; the swarm of frogs seems to carry out a ritual discussion with their frenzied clamor;

the parched earth, scorched by the rain, emits a fragrance like that of sprinkled parched grain; and the Lord of Light (the sun), though difficult to perceive, is made manifest by the smile of the lotus-ponds.
The same applies to others as well.
Furthermore,
it is said in the world that the *dhūlīkadamba* flower blooms during the summer season.
Upon the arrival of the rainy season, that very same cluster of raindrops becomes a showering thundercloud.
For example:

"O Blue-throated One, do you not indeed long for the arrival of the battle-cloud, which greyens the quarters of the sky with its mass of dust, adorns the bow of the Lord of the Gods with streaks of red, and releases lightning as its blazing weapon?"
That species which is born in the water and is called "mud-born" becomes full of fragrance and frequented by bees during the great festival of autumn.
For example:
"The net of creepers, naturally pervaded by a mature fragrance and possessing large buds whose knots were burst open by the brilliance of thick dewdrops, unfolded.
The water, marked by the coils of serpents, suddenly became like the bed of another ocean—having various swans for its pillows and the moon for its pillow, white with moonlight."
Some maintain that there is even a slight persistence [of the previous season] in the *ketakī* flower;
as it is said:
"The autumn season was indicated by the *ketakī* flowers, grey with pollen."
He was like the days that have newly arrived with their feet, copper-red as lotuses.
If the persistence of autumnal phenomena— the bows together with the *kuruṇṭaka* flowers—
is seen even in the mouth of winter, then the poetic conventions of the poets are no longer seen.
When the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons are treated as one, there is simply the persistence of all the characteristics [of the year].
And it has been said:
"A year consists of twelve months."
"The five seasons [are established], with the winter and the cool season combined as one.

A fragrant spring, possessing a variegated splendor, should be depicted through the presence of *marubaka*, *damanaka*, and *puṇnāga* flowers, and by the recurrence of the *liṅga* flower, as well as through the recurrence of the *kunda* jasmine.

“In the houses of the Vāhīka youths, the *damanaka* plant bears clusters of blossoms to be worn as ear-ornaments; in the wind fragrant with *marubaka*, the intoxication of the village women becomes manifest.

Immediately following its breaking, the resinous sap, dripping with warm streams and accompanied by *sahakāra* flowers, creates moon-like reflections upon the surface of the water in the serpent’s drinking bowl.”
Distraught at the tamāla tree with its budding flowers, anxious before the kiṅkirāta, sorrowful for long at the red aśoka, and squinting his eyes at the fully blossomed campaka—
the traveler, though weary from fatigue, approaches with longing, shaking with his ragged garment the swarm of bees greedy for the fresh nectar and buzzing harshly against his ears.
Or for example:

"The gentle breeze, shaking the sandalwood trees on the banks of the Kāverī and scattering the nectar of the jasmine clusters, causes the curls on the foreheads of the Lāṭī women— who have been disheveled by the pulling of their lovers' play— to dance, as they fall from root to tip over their straight brows."
In the same way, there is also another persistence [of fragrance]:
"The persistences of the *vicakila*, *kerala*, *pāṭali*, and *campaka* flowers occur in summer;
and therein, some also desire the *marubaka*, which arises in the winter season."
For example:

"A smiling *śirīṣa* flower at the ear, *vicakila* garlands upon the head, *pāṭalinī* flowers at the neck, a necklace of lotus stalks encircling the arms, dark lotus fibers coiled around the wrists, sandalwood water joyfully applied to the breasts, eyes with the pigment of *nāñjiṣṭha* faded, and limbs moist with dripping water— victorious is this summer attire of the deer-eyed women!"
And as it is said:
"The *śirīṣa* flower on the ear vies with the needle of fresh *kuśa* grass; the *marubaka* wreath and the *pāṭala* garland are upon the neck;
yet the indescribable attire of the beautiful women, born from the change of day, shines forth, its eyes closed by the moisture of fresh water."
Thus are other examples.

"The occurrence and recurrence of the seasons have been indicated here merely by way of illustration; O virtuous ones, observe the remainder with your own intelligence. How much can we say by naming each one?"
"In various regions, a reversal of the essential nature of things is observed;
therefore, one should not adhere to that [convention] too rigidly, for what is composed by poets is our authority here."
A flower is useful in six ways: through its beauty, fragrance, scent, stalk, fruit, and worship; that which is devoid of these is useless.
For example:
"The flower that was formed in the first month must be made into a young fruit in the next;
in the one following that, it should be brought to maturity, and in the one after that, it should be perfected by ripening."
This procedure for those produced from trees has been observed; for those that are creepers or fruits, there is no great delay.
For them, the limit is only two months; this is the time required for flowering, fruiting, and the process of ripening.
There is fruit that is deceptive in one way, deceptive externally, and deceptive both externally and internally;
likewise, there is fruit that is entirely deceptive, deceptive in many ways, and free from deception.
In this context, the *lakucha* and others have an internal pretext (*antarvyāja*), while the *moca* (plantain) and others have an external pretext (*bahirvyāja*).
The mango (*āmra*) and others have both types of pretext (*ubhayavyāja*), and the *kakubha* and others constitute the "pretext of all" (*sarvavyāja*).
The jackfruit and others possess many deceptive qualities (*vyāja*), while the blue wood-apple and others are free from deception (*nirvyāja*);
thus, the distinction among all fruits should be understood by poets as being sixfold.
One should compose the seasons in literary works according to their divisions of one, two, three, and so forth, either collectively or individually,
in regular order or in reverse order.
There is no fault of transgression for a poet who touches upon the path of meaning;
rather, in such and such a manner, a certain transposition may become an ornament.
For one devoid of critical investigation, even an ornament becomes a flaw;
yet for a vigilant poet, even a flaw becomes an ornament.
Thus has been shown the nature of the division of time;
here the poet is greatly deluded, while here the great poet is perfected.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Division of Time," in the first section, *Kavirahasya* (The Secret of the Poet), of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* composed by Rājaśekhara. This concludes the first section, *Kavirahasya*, within the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā*.
